speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many concerned citizens in my riding of Grey-Simcoe and surrounding area have brought to my attention the Bell Canada proposal which would change the billing procedure now in force to a system whereby the customer will be charged for individually made telephone calls. It has been correctly pointed out that this would create undue hardship for seniors, the handicapped, low-income families on fixed income, and those who rely heavily on the telephone as their main source of communication.
As well, seniors and handicapped persons often have to order medicines, groceries, et cetera, by telephone, when no transportation is available. They have to consult and report to their physicians more often than others, and the cost of individual calls would be astronomical.
This would cause extra monetary worries for those who can ill afford the extra cost, and would result in a loss of community involvement to seniors and others who have continued to keep involved in church groups, service clubs and so on, by telephone.
Therefore I call upon the Government to exercise every possible influence on Bell Canada not to proceed with such a proposal which would prove very detrimental to all Canadians.

subtopic: TAX DEPARTMENT'S TREATMENT OF VANCOUVER SYMPHONY
TAX DEPARTMENT'S TREATMENT OF VANCOUVER SYMPHONY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for years there have been discrepancies in the income tax treatment of musicians who are members of Canada's symphony orchestras. Some are treated as employees and are thus denied deduction of expenses and capital cost allowance, while others are considered to be self-employed and are allowed proper deductions in arriving at net income for tax purposes.
Even though the Subcommittee on the Taxation of Visual and Performing Artists and Writers was considering this very subject and has since recommended amendments to the Income Tax Act to allow deduction of expenses incurred by symphony musicians, the Minister, in the meantime, changed the treatment for Toronto Symphony members, leaving only the Vancouver Symphony members as employees denied deduction of expenses.
The Minister has received copies of the Vancouver Symphony Society telegram that was sent to the Chairman of the Subcommittee outlining the injustices and discrimination against western Canadians. I appeal to the Minister to implement the needed changes in treatment immediately, so that a measure of equity will be restored to the application of the Income Tax Act.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this day and age of advanced technology in information gathering and recording it is a regressive and backward practice to be a slave to a traditional voting procedure in this House which necessitates an individual personal response of standing and then bowing to the Chair in sequence to one's announced name.
As a medical doctor I feel that such a mode of voting, when numerous votes are scheduled on a given day, can be a type of psychological and physical torture to Members. Being confined to their seats for hours places considerable physical and emotional stress on Members, regardless of their baseline state of health. It is unwise to push Hon. Members to, or beyond, their physiological limits. These limits are marginal in those with underlying medical difficulties.
In other words, this traditional mode of voting in the House, carried out to the extreme as it was the night before last and through the early hours of the morning, can be a form of personal physical and mental assault on Members, and thus is no longer an acceptable procedure. I strongly recommend that the parliamentary committee which reviews the rules of procedure and the Standing Orders of the House should consider the introduction in the House of an electronically activated recording mechanism for voting, such as the one used by the United States House of Representatives.

ECONOMIC POLICY OF PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE AND LIBERAL PARTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are seeing higher interest rates to protect the Canadian dollar, which is falling out of sight. The reason is that money is being sucked out of the country to the United States.
News reports this morning quoted the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) as saying that he approves of the economic policies being pursued in the United States. No one should be surprised that the Leader of the Opposition stands firmly behind Ronald Reagan, but everyone should be aware of what it means. One of the reasons for the growth of the American economy is a level of military spending which stands at the highest in the history of the world.
It is time to stop and look at what this massive military spending in the United States-and perhaps later in Canada- is doing. Helmut Schmidt, a former Chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany and a defender of the Atlantic Alliance, made a statement recently in the New York "Review of Books". He said that because of this massive military spending:
The high interest rate policy-the highest real interest rates in centuries- dictated by the Reagan deficits let the world's richest economy become the world's greatest importer of capital. This has been occurring at the expense of real investment... and therefore employment in the other industrialized countries and in all the developing countries that do not export oil.
The policy of the Leader of the Opposition and of the Turner Liberals applauds the fact that it has cost thousands of jobs in Canada and driven poorer nations to the verge of bankruptcy. That is the kind of policy which they both want to adopt in Canada, and it has to stop.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I obviously have not had the time to consider at any length the implications of the statement you just made. subsubtopic: MR. CLARKE-ALLEGED UNPARLIAMENTARY LANGUAGE OF MR. TRUDEAU

Members would accept it. The Chair is quite prepared to look at situations where unparliamentary language is used. If Hon. Members have a view that unparliamentary language is used, the Chair is quite prepared to look at situations.
However, the Chair must be expected to exercise consistency. The Chair has overlooked the term "fabrication" so often that to ask the Chair in this instance to judge it unparliamentary is to ask for a substantial break in recent practice of the House.

subsubtopic: MR. CLARKE-ALLEGED UNPARLIAMENTARY LANGUAGE OF MR. TRUDEAU
speechtext:

subsubtopic: MR. CLARKE-ALLEGED UNPARLIAMENTARY LANGUAGE OF MR. TRUDEAU

speechtext:
That is not fair. The Chair has tried to use discretion and good judgment. I can remember on one occasion the Chair ruled an expression about a chief reptile unparliamentary. The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) is laughing because he well recalls the occasion. Let me quote from the latest edition of Erskine May, the Twentieth Edition, page viii of the Preface:
Such a list can never be exhaustive and its value to the Chair appears increasingly doubtful. subsubtopic: MR. CLARKE-ALLEGED UNPARLIAMENTARY LANGUAGE OF MR. TRUDEAU
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my only concern is that the term "a complete fabrication" is synonymous with calling a person a liar. While other words may be used, I know that the word "lying" has not been allowed. It is really synonymous.

speechtext: The Chair has accepted "fabrication" in place of "lying". When the Chair has asked a Member to withdraw that word, the Member has said: "I withdraw the accusation that so and so is lying; it is just a fabrication that he uttered".

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. CLARKE-ALLEGED UNPARLIAMENTARY LANGUAGE OF MR. TRUDEAU

subsubtopic: MR. CLARKE-ALLEGED UNPARLIAMENTARY LANGUAGE OF MR. TRUDEAU

speakeroldname: Hon. Yvon Pinard (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. CLARKE-ALLEGED UNPARLIAMENTARY LANGUAGE OF MR. TRUDEAU
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of Members in this House who think they know everything. They are behaving like real aliborons. I repeat: they are behaving like aliborons.
Words should be considered in the proper context. I think it is wrong to take a word out of context, interpret it subjectively, and thus give us an erroneous interpretation.
I think the Chair is right in saying that lists of words that go back to 1958, and I see here the word "ignoramus". Apparently, it is unparliamentary to call someone an ignoramus. To say that is to say somebody is ignorant. I think this is absurd and out-dated. I think we have all heard expressions that shock us a bit more than that one. In any case, people who are claiming today that the word "fabrication" is unparliamentary do not know what they are talking about.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. CLARKE-ALLEGED UNPARLIAMENTARY LANGUAGE OF MR. TRUDEAU
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to use up too much time on this matter but there is an important element to it. I am concerned about the kind of advice that you are getting, not only from members of the New Democratic Party who are now suggesting that we accept the use of the word "lying" and "liar", but from the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) who is condoning the use of derisive references to Members of this Chamber.
I know that you, Mr. Speaker, as a Member of Parliament who has served for some years now, will fully understand that what we are talking about now is the integrity of this institution. We are not talking about whether individuals are worthy of serving in this particular institution but whether we are going to have a poisonous aspect to our debates and an element of unreasonable personal accusations in debate. We want to avoid that. We want to debate the issues.
There are strong feelings held with respect to the issues and with respect to the personalities in the House. I do not think that this is a flippant matter at all. I do not think that the way we address each other and address this Chamber is a laughing matter at all. I do not think these matters are cute or funny at all.
I suggest that we get the kind of legislature we deserve by virtue of our activities and the way in which Members of Parliament conduct themselves. There is a difference between levity and accusations against another Member. I think that should always be in the back of the minds of Members of Parliament, even as we come to the end of this Parliament.
The important consideration is that this is a great country and a great institution and we are only worthy of serving here
June 22, 1984

if we in fact respect each other despite our political differences.

subsubtopic: MR. CLARKE-ALLEGED UNPARLIAMENTARY LANGUAGE OF MR. TRUDEAU
speechtext: I cannot help but agree with everything that the Hon. Member has said. I will review the matter.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not at all want to prolong this. I believe there may well be a problem for Private Members of the House to which I want to draw your attention, although I am sure you are already seized of it.
The practice has been that when there is a suspicion of unparliamentary language, either the Chair intervenes or a Member raises a point of order based upon the list at hand. I quite understand that the passage of time may have ruled as acceptable language which might not have been acceptable at an earlier time and that the list may be in need of changes. However, if the Speaker needs a list for his interventions on these matters, so do Private Members need a list for our interventions on the matter.
My simple request would be that if there is to be a change in the list or in the principles determining language that will be parliamentary and unparliamentary, those of us who sit in the House and might be either guilty of using that language or accused of being guilty of using that language would like to know what the new standards are. That is the extent of my request.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I just want to say that I am quite prepared to speak following the Hon. Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday).

Mr. Speaker, I am certainly pleased to lead off this third reading debate. I thought perhaps we might have heard from the Parliamentary Secretary initially. I am hoping that he will have something to say on this Bill that will be news for us. There are some areas that were raised in the committee stage which we had hoped the Minister or the Parliamentary Secretary might have addressed this morning.
Let me say first that I am a little disappointed that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) is not here today. It would seem to me that a Bill as important as this one on pensions, about which the Minister from time to time has shown such concern over the years, is not one she sees fit to bring into the House herself at third reading. She may very well have some important business to attend to today and I am in no way denigrating the presence today of her Parliamentary Secretary. In my ten years in the House and with the experience I have had with Ministers and Parliamentary Secretaries, there has never been a Parliamentary Secretary more co-operative with us in the Opposition and easy to get along with in a non-partisan way than the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacLellan). We appreciate his co-operation because occasionally we are sometimes too partisan on certain important issues.
Be that as it may, it is disappointing to note that the Minister is not here. I thought she would have some rather

June 22, 1984
Old Age Security Act
interesting announcements about some new thoughts or attitudes she might have toward addressing the income security problems of the disabled, particularly those who receive workmen's compensation benefits or compensation itself. However, we hope the Parliamentary Secretary will address that.
As we move into third reading, the purpose of this Bill is to make amendments to the Old Age Security Act, and in particular to change the maximum amounts payable under the guaranteed income supplement. None of us will dispute the need and we are glad the Government has seen its way clear to bring in something that will bring to a more reasonable level the payments made under the guaranteed income supplement Act for certain pensioners.
In addition the Bill does provide a number of technical amendments that are certainly non-controversial, such as amendments regarding residency requirements with respect to retroactivity for people who have, for one reason or another, not made their application at the usual time for benefits. I do not think we want to debate that or indicate any question about the wisdom of those technical amendments.
As for the general purpose of the Bill, Mr. Speaker, we in the Official Opposition support it completely and as a result we are willing to support this Bill. But I think it is incumbent upon us to point out to the Government and to the people that this Bill does not really address the whole problem of pension reform. When one considers the amount of talk we have had from the Government for years and years, going back at least five years, and the number of times we have heard the Minister herself speak about the need for pension reform, we would have thought that by this time, particularly with an election in the offing, we would have had something more definitive and substantive regarding the question of pensions.
Let us look at what Bill C-40 does address and at the very limited way it addresses the subject of appropriate increases to the guaranteed income supplement. The actual amount of the increase will be $25 effective in a few days, on July 1, and another $25 effective on December 1, for a total of $50. I will not become involved in giving statistics in this third reading debate. However, I remind the House, the Parliamentary Secretary and through him the Minister, that when the OAS and GIS were originally brought into effect in this country there was an existing relationship between the maximum combined payment available and the average industrial wage. The maximum payment available under OAS and GIS amounted to approximately 20 per cent of the average industrial wage. One might have argued that it should have been more, but nonetheless that was the figure accepted at that time. It is interesting to note that today even with a $50 increase, the level is only 14 per cent of the average industrial wage in Canada.
The Government could have avoided completely the necessity of this catch-up Bill if it had treated our senior citizens more properly from the beginning. Having given them an initial payment which amounted to 20 per cent of the average
industrial wage, why did it not see fit in the interim-and it has been in government most of the time since then-to maintain that ratio? Rather, it let it slip down to 14 per cent, as is the case now, just because it refused to increase the payments sufficiently to maintain that ratio in light of the inflation we have suffered. It is disappointing that we have to deal with this Bill when it could have been completely avoided had the Government maintained its original promise of a payment sufficient to provide 20 per cent of the average industrial wage.
Let me look at the delays of the Government in most recent years, particularly this year, in bringing forth such a simple amendment to the Old Age Security Act. The Minister has repeatedly said over the years that pensions were one of her prime concerns. We took her word on that. It was mentioned in the Speech from the Throne in December, 1983 that it would be a priority of the Government to increase the benefits payable to pensioners, particularly those entitled to GIS benefits. Then we had the Budget on February 15 of this year. At that time, over four months ago, a commitment was made by the Government to bring in amendments to the Old Age Security Act which would boost inadequate payments with respect to GIS benefits. Having waited from February 15, we in the Official Opposition thought it was ridiculous to have to wait longer before bringing the subject before the House of Commons for debate.
Among the subjects which we as members of the Official Opposition thought had high priority was the subject of pension reform. Therefore we used one of our very precious Opposition days or allotted days on May 10, almost three months after the Government had promised in its Budget Speech that there would be amendments, to bring the whole subject matter before the House for debate as nothing had been brought forward by the Government. The Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) and the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), among others, led off in a very effective debate drawing to the attention of the House and to the people of Canada the failure of the Government to deal adequately with Canadian pensioners. Despite our exhortations at that time, we had to wait until May 29 for first reading of a very simple Bill which effectively offered an extra $25 in July and another $25 in December as increases in the benefits to be paid under the GIS provisions of the Old Age Security Act.
There was a lesser delay with respect to the presentation of the Bill for second reading on June 4. Of course, at that point the Government realized that time was running out. If one looks at the time sequence and the delays which the Government built into the delivery of Bill C-40 just to provide an extra $50 in payments, one realizes that the Government had ulterior motives. It was more interested in something other than offering senior citizens $50. It was more interested in providing something which it thought would be of benefit come election time. Therefore, within a month or two of the probable dissolution of Parliament, we find a simple Bill before the House which could have been before us late in
June 22, 1984

February or early in March if the Government had been really serious and anxious to use it for other than ulterior motives.
We did not delay the Bill at second reading. We thought it was a very essential amendment to the Old Age Security Act with which we should deal as quickly as possible for the benefit of senior citizens. We were anxious to see the Bill reach committee stage, which followed fairly promptly after second reading because the Government had no alternative if it wanted the Bill passed before the end of this Parliament. If my memory is correct, the committee met on three different days to consider Bill C-40.
A few moments ago I took the trouble to total the number of hours which we were allowed to discuss the Bill at committee stage. According to my calculation, it came to slightly under three hours or very close to three hours during the course of three different days. Witnesses appeared before the committee, including the Minister herself, which we appreciated. It provided us with an opportunity to direct questions to her. She did a reasonably good job and made a good attempt at trying to answer our questions. There were some to which she could not reply, such as the question dealing with the relationship between workmen's compensation pension benefits that 25,000 Canadians receive and how they will suffer either a complete or partial reduction in their GIS payments. Of course, the Minister acknowledged the problem. It was one area on which she promised further review and discussion with her colleagues. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will be able to elucidate today some of the thinking of his Cabinet colleagues who have expressed disappointment at what turned up regarding the earlier amendments to the Income Tax Act which worked to the disadvantage of these 25,000 Canadians.
While we had the Minister and her senior officials concerned with the welfare side of her Department and with the pension plan before us in committee-and I must say that they gave good testimony and answered our questions in a reasonable manner-I must say there was one item lacking in the evidence at that time. I am referring to the results of the studies which had taken place between the federal department and various provincial departments with respect to income security for disabled persons. The big disappointment was that on a subject matter as important to Canadians as pension reform, we had a Bill which dealt only with a slight increase in GIS payments. We did not have a chance when dealing with a subject as important as pension reform to have other witnesses before the committee, obviously because of lack of time. That was probably done deliberately because the Government held off first reading of this Bill until so late in the session that it was impossible for the committee to discuss at greater length some of the important issues which flow out of the whole subject of pension reform.
I know the Parliamentary Secretary will tell us that a task force dealt with this, and that is true. Unfortunately, the Minister has refused at this point in time to implement any of the recommendations coming out of the task force other than
Old Age Security Act
the matter of the increase in the guaranteed income supplement.
I have alluded to the fact that this Bill, good as it is for what it does, is completely inadequate as far as pension reform is concerned. I made reference to the fact that in the last five years the Minister has repeatedly said how important she feels pension reform is, that we had a national conference two or three years ago and a task force, as well as dealing with it in Parliament. Out of all those efforts in Parliament, in the private sector and at the national level by way of the national conference held in Ottawa, we still have no definitive or substantive legislation being brought forward by this Government that will bring meaningful reform to our pension system.
There is an increasing need and urgency for this. The Minister voices this and acknowledges that fact. We have to admit that we have seen what happens when we have a big bulge in our population at the elementary and secondary school levels, the pressure that places on society in general to accommodate that increase in population at that age group.
Today the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. MacLaren) alluded to the massive increases we have had in the labour force and the pressures that brings to bear upon our society. Here we have this Liberal Government refusing to look ahead to the days when we will have that same bulge in our senior citizen ranks of those over 65.
If we do not take cognizance of that now in a meaningful way and do something other than talk about it, we will be in great difficulty in a few years, the year 2000 for example, when we have this massive increase in the number of people who will be in that age group. It will require not only pension reform and support for them in their older days, but support will also be required for their health care.
This reminds me that not many months ago we debated Bill C-3, the Canada Health Act. We had there the same situation as we have now. That Bill was brought in by the Government allegedly to improve the health care of Canadians. When we got to studying that Bill, we found it was the same situation that we now have with amendments to the Old Age Security Act. It was nothing more than a very technical amendment to the provision of health care in Canada whereby the provinces would be penalized if they did not fulfil certain obligations that the federal Government thought they should fulfil.
The Canada Health Act, like Bill C-40 before us today, refused to address the future needs of the health care of Canadians. It ties in with this same bulge in our population. When this same bulge hits those aged 65 and onwards, we will have massive increases in cost vis-a-vis our senior citizens. The increase will be in the order of 50 per cent above what we have now in proportion to the general population. It is something we have to look at well in advance of being faced with the crisis.
This is the second time within six months that this Liberal Government is bringing in picayune legislation to address a very minimal problem in the health care situation or pension problem situation. It is not tackling the real problems that

June 22, 1984
Old Age Security Act
exist, namely what we are going to do for health care and pensions when this big bulge in our population hits those aged 65 and onward.
On March 17 of last year, about 15 months ago, the Minister gave the "cold, hard facts" about our pension needs in Canada. She was saying at that time essentially what I am saying now. She recognized the fact. I do not deny that she realizes what I am saying. I am sure she would be the first to admit it. She acknowledged then that the cold hard facts demanded that there be some pension reform in Canada. Fifteen months later we do not have one substantive change to our pension system which recognizes these cold hard facts that she spoke about, other than this simple social assistance increase. All we get in this Bill is an increase of S50. There are no new ideas in it, no new approaches to the pension system of this country. It is a simple increase in a monetary sense prior to an election to try and convince Canadians that the Liberal Party is a good Party and that it will give them a little extra money. They have refused to tell Canadians that we need more than that kind of a change to our system. We need fundamental changes to our pension system that recognize the difficulties this country is getting into today.
This ties in very closely with the subject of pensions. I will not get into a lot of figures. As I said earlier, third reading is not the appropriate time for that. However, let me remind the Minister and her Parliamentary Secretary that there is a lot of talk about the poverty line. The Minister tries to pretend that what she is doing by way of this $50 increase will make some magic increase in the level of income for those unfortunate Canadians who live below the poverty line. It may be if you apply averages and take those from the rural areas and smaller municipalities and average them with those in the urban areas, she may be able to claim that Bill C-40 will bring Canadian pensioners up to the poverty line. The figures we have do not suggest that at all.
Even with this increase in the minimum that will be payable under the OA/GIS payments, if you take pensioners who are eligible for those payments living in cities of 20,000 or more, those people would be receiving something in the order of $1,900 under the poverty line. Therefore, it is not fair to say that Canadian pensioners will be brought up to the level of the so-called poverty line. Tens of thousands of Canadians will still be under the poverty line, particularly those who live in urban areas. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will take note of that. If he has figures to disprove that fact, we would like to know about it.
The other major disappointment and inadequate component or feature of this Bill is that it has failed to address the severe problems of the old age pensioner in this country who is female. The Minister was one of the first in this House to deplore the inadequate pension that was and is being paid to women in so many facets of our society. There is no area that is neglected more, even by this Government, than pensions for women. My colleague from Kingston and the Islands probably more than any other person in this Chamber throughout the years has attempted to bring to the attention of the House and
the Government the fact that this is one of the great deficiencies in our pension system in Canada. I refer to the fact that the women of this country are not adequately covered by appropriate pensions. That is true not only for women who are in the workforce, some of whom are obviously better covered than others, and women are more inadequately covered than men, but it is true as well for housewives.
The biggest deficiency in the pension system exists for the two million or three million Canadian women who are housewives and who do their day-to-day work on behalf of the country and on behalf of their families in the home. No provision has yet been made by the Government to supply any kind of pension for those women. That should be a real priority for any Government but this Government, after talking for years and years about the need for pension reform and after the Minister having been aware for the last 15 months of the cold hard facts, has still not been able to bring before the House any legislation to correct this problem.
I suppose the Canadian people realize that this is one of the deficiencies of the present Liberal Government. I daresay that the Canadian people are now making up their minds and in fact may have already made up their minds that the time has come for a change in government if they are to receive the kind of legislation they are looking for. I think the women of Canada have long since realized that the present Government is not interested in providing that kind of legislation. The Government has had years to do so. Nothing has come forward other than seminars, conferences and parliamentary debate. Nothing meaningful has been done for the women of Canada with regard to pensions.
Let me now turn to another subject to which I alluded briefly a few moments ago. This represents another of the gross deficiencies in this Bill and it is the need for pensions for the disabled and the handicapped. I had the privilege of serving for three years on the Special Committee of this House on the Disabled and the Handicapped. I thought it was one of the most enlightening, rewarding and satisfying experiences I have had in my ten years in the House of Commons. This committee was headed up by the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Smith) who was an excellent chairman of that committee. He gave good leadership to the committee. I would also like to give him credit for the nature of the report that came out of that committee. That report has received what I would deem to be unjustified criticism from some Members of the House because of its alleged elaborateness.
I think the committee deserves credit for coming up with some 130 recommendations, some of which dealt with the subject of pensions and income security. Among those recommendations were something in the order of 11 recommendations that dealt significantly with income security for disabled people. I think with some chagrin that Members on both sides of the House have shown some disappointment in that report. As well, the administration of the House has made some
June 22, 1984

suggestions regarding reforms to approval of committee expenditures, suggestions which give me cause for alarm. The administration has made these suggestions because we spent some extra money to produce a very effective report, a report with an innovative layout and one which included a number of pictures of disabled people designed to show that a disabled person was not different, Mr. Speaker, from you or me. Because we included these pictures and because our format was innovative and probably used a few more pieces of paper and some coloured photographs which had not traditionally been used in parliamentary reports, attempts are now being made to cut back on expenditures on subsequent committee reports.
I believe that committee report was probably the most effective report that has ever been produced by a special parliamentary committee. It is a report which has received world-wide recognition from groups of disabled people. There have been three printings of that report, indicative of the fact that when it was first seen it brought to the attention of Canadians the need for some action in this area and the fact that it was so well received by the people who understood the need in that area that there was an increased demand for copies of the report. Parenthetically, as it were, I wanted to bring this up in debate today because it is germane to today's discussion that that special committee on the disabled and the handicapped spent a significant amount of time on the subject of income security for Canadians who are disabled. Among that group of disabled Canadians are many who are over the age of 65 and are eligible for the OAS and the GIS benefits.
One of the things that our committee tried to get across in its report-and if I can brag for a moment, perhaps no one pushed this point more than I did-was the need for the acceptance of the fact that disabled people have expenses over and above the expenses of those of us who are able-bodied. If we are to provide adequate income support for those people when they are in their senior years, we must provide them with more than the traditional OAS and GIS benefits. Those benefits are not sufficient. They need more benefits because they have added expenses. That is one of the recommendations that the Government has completely ignored up until now in its assessment of the report of the Committee on the Disabled and the Handicapped.
I would like to stress the fact that there is a real need for the Government to look into the matter of how we shall adequately reimburse the handicapped of the country, particularly with regard to income security and the acknowledgement of the fact that they have increased expenditures. Along those same lines my colleague, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), when he spoke at second reading, and several others including the colleague of the Parliamentary Secretary, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall), have spoken of the fact that senior citizens who now receive GIS as well as worker's compensation benefits because of disabilities suffered years ago will suffer a loss of income because they must now take those compensation benefits into account when calculating their GIS benefits.
Old Age Security Act
In closing, let me touch upon two or three more points. First, the lack of adequate coverage in the pension system partly stems from the fact that the results of the Government's economic policies have been catastrophic. The Government has failed to introduce any kind of economic policy to make it possible to pay adequate pension incomes to our senior citizens. As acknowledged by Dr. Larkin Kerwin, the President of the National Research Council, the Liberal Government saw fit in its early years following the Second World War to set a policy of spending no money on research and development. In order to have a sound economy today, it would have been necessary to make such expenditures. That is why Japan's economy is so good today and why ours is so inadequate as compared to those of the United States and Japan.
Had the Government adopted different policies some years ago and spent some money developing the economy in the country, there would have been a more adequate pension system than the one that exists today. Instead of that, the money that was available to the Government was spent on bailouts for Maislin, bailouts for de Havilland and the purchasing of Petrofina gas stations when it could have been spent on pensions for senior citizens.
Let me conclude by saying that we in the Opposition feel that Bill C-40 needs to be passed. Indeed, pensioners are in desperate need of this $50 increase. That increase is perfectly fine, but let us not forget that the real purpose of this Bill, coming before the House as it does months and months after the Government recognized the problem, coming before the House one month before the House is to be prorogued, is political opportunism. The Bill was brought before the House for one reason only, and that is because it was a matter of political expediency for the Government to tell the senior citizens of Canada that the Liberal Government allegedly cares about them and will offer those who are entitled to receive GIS benefits another $50 per month. I do not think the people of Canada will be fooled by that kind of legislation when the election rolls around in the next few months.

Mr. Speaker, I am not sure if the Hon. Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday) is right. It is entirely possible that the measures which are being introduced are being introduced for strictly political reasons. If that is the case, I am not satisfied with the measures. I would not be satisfied with those measures even if that was not the case. Quite frankly, any government which thinks it can buy the votes of the Canadian public with $600 a year is dreaming. Therefore, I do not much care what the motivation was, because the end result is inadequate.
First, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Oxford. He covered a variety of different legitimate and related concerns. I was particularly interested in his comments with regard to the plight of elderly women who are single. Indeed, that is a legitimate concern and should be a major concern of the Government. As well, I concur with the suggestion that he made at the end of his speech concerning the

June 22, 1984
Old Age Security Act
matter of financial support for those who fall into the category of being disabled. That matter has not been adequately addressed by the Government. We must find new and innovative ways to provide additional support. The majority of those individuals who fall into that unfortunate category will not receive benefits from this particular measure. I mention those two items because I found them interesting and worth listening to in terms of their substance.
The Bill which is before us is totally inadequate. It is another example of the piecemeal approach of the Government to matters of financial support. In many ways it is misleading inasmuch as it left the impression-one which was first brought forward when the suggestion was made-that there would be an increase in pension levels. The inference that Canadian pensioners would benefit in the over-all, rather than simply those who happen to be single and on GIS, was there. It is unfortunate.
No one in the House would deny that my hon. colleague from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has been in the forefront of the debate on the inadequacies of pensions in Canada since the time before which many of us were born. Had it not been for his tenacity, his strength of character and his capacity to influence by the spoken word the direction which government should take, the inadequate levels of pensions which we now have would have been even more inadequate. I know that if my colleague from Winnipeg North Centre were here today, he would be the first on his feet trying to convince the House of Commons to do what I am proposing should be done-that is, to immediately increase the base level of the Old Age Security.
It must be recognized in Canada that this piecemeal approach to income maintenance will not satisfy today's recipients. Neither will it satisfy the large numbers of people who will ultimately become the recipients of Old Age Security. I say to the Parliamentary Secretary, in the absence of the Minister, I do not deny for one moment that the providing of adequate pensions to Canadians is costly. I am prepared to accept the fact that there will be some in society who will want to argue that the cost is too high. But I want to make it clear that I neither subscribe to nor support that view. I find it offensive. When people who have the means and find themselves quite comfortable in their existence can argue the point, as they frequently do, that the cost of guaranteeing others less fortunate than themselves an adequate level of income during their retirement years is too high and impossible to provide, we must rethink the ways in which we spend tax dollars. If it is true that the current treasury cannot find the money to provide levels of pension for those who retire and who have built this country, and if it is true that we have to do that, then there is no time more suitable for starting than now. The Government is charged with a responsibility and that responsibility goes beyond its terms of office. The Government and Members of Parliament must assume that the actions which they take on behalf of the public of Canada will be beneficial in the long term of office, and that successive Parliaments will be supportive of the new direction that should be proposed. We must
build into our pension system, not only the adequate base of which I speak, but a means of ensuring that those who retire and those who must exist on pensions are able to keep pace with the ever-increasing cost of living. I am prepared to be in the forefront of those who say that, whatever the cost is, it must be borne. However we find the money, we must find it. Therefore, we must start that process.
There have been reports on this subject. My colleague and friend, the Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Miller), sat on a committee which discussed the problems of pensions, which included the interrelationship between private and public pensions and the interrelationship between the Old Age Security system and the Canada Pension Plan, together with all of the assistance programs which flow from that-the guaranteed income supplement, all the way through to supplementary benefits which are given by certain of the provinces to the aged.
The question arises as to how to deal with the contribution which is made by housewives. What is that contribution to the over-all growth of society? How can it be measured when there is no clear income which flows to those women? I do not think that anyone has been able adequately to come to grips with that question. There have been a number of suggestions as to how it can be done, but the one thing which worries me is that there does not appear to be the parliamentary political will to proceed with those suggestions. We can find time in the House of Commons to do any number of things some of them valuable, some somewhat less valuable. But on a question as fundamental and as basic as guaranteeing a woman who has worked at home, raised a family and looked after the household an income at the time of retirement, due to age, loss of husband or partner, we should provide that woman with the opportunity to live in a society of which she has been so much a part. For some reason that question does not seem important enough for the House of Commons. For many women in this country, it is the single most important question that they face.
It worries me, Mr. Speaker, that we end up dealing with a $50 a month increase for a select few individuals in need. It is a $50 a month increase which, no doubt every single one of them will be delighted to receive, but it is a $50 increase which will in fact be totally inadequate at this time to meet their needs. We can find time to deal with that but we cannot find time to deal with the basic and fundamental question of how we can establish an income maintenance program. Perhaps it is time for us to look at how we can guarantee people an income. Perhaps the whole thought process must be changed. Perhaps the way pensions per se have been allocated in the past is not the right way. Perhaps we have to move towards the adoption of a guaranteed annual income program, which can be more easily funded, I say to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans). These things are difficult, but I think he will agree that we can work them out.
I believe this House of Commons should be meeting in session and trying to find a solution to a guaranteed annual
June 22, 1984

income. I believe that is important. We would then begin to address a number of questions, not only the problems of pensioners, but the question of giving the disabled an income which would begin to meet their needs. We would begin to address the question of those who are single, who go through their lives without partners, who perhaps do not have an adequate private pension arrangement. We would speak to unemployment in many ways and to the question of early retirement. What happens to people when they get to an age when they are physically unable to do the work they have always done? Yet these same people continue to have obligations which demand an income sufficient to meet those obligations. What do you say to someone who has been a labourer in a field of work which is onerous and physically demanding when that person reaches the age of 50 or 60 and time has taken its toll? They can no longer continue to climb to the top of a high building to put the bolts in place which hold the girders. What do you say to that person when he gets laid off or he cannot climb up there any more on a daily basis and does not qualify for a pension or any kind of assistance? To tell him to go find another job is ridiculous.
I feel we are evading the real question. The real question before us today, surely, is how we can make sure through legislative action that people who live and work in Canada- and I include people who work at home-are able throughout their lives to have a base income level which will be sufficient to meet their basic needs. I am not talking about extravagance; I am talking about basic needs. That is never talked about and we must do so. The question is always, can we afford to give another small supplement to this group? Can we afford to subsidize this or that group? Can we extend UIC a little for another group? Can we in some way meet the peculiar needs of one group of individuals who happen to have peculiar needs which are different from the needs of the balance of society? Frankly, I believe in doing it that way, but we tend to approach the topic in a piecemeal fashion and, therefore, lose sight of what the real problem is.
The real problem for people basically is, how do they get enough income to meet their needs? That is why they work; that is why they need unemployment benefits when they cannot work; that is why they need workmen's compensation when they hurt; that is why they get a pension when they retire; that is why we provide an allowance when they are unable to work and do not qualify for any other assistance; and that is why Canada Pension Plan was brought in and extended to meet the needs of those who are ill for long periods of time. It was not done on a humanitarian basis-or perhaps it was partly. It was certainly not done primarily on a humanitarian basis. It was done because we recognized that people's financial needs are fundamental and, therefore, must be addressed.
What I am really saying today is that it is always disappointing to be handed a piece of legislation which-and I say this quite categorically-is no doubt being welcomed by those who will receive the benefit, but which does not address the real problem. Obviously, any little bit of help is going to be supported by everyone. It is certainly better than leaving
Old Age Security Act
things the way they are. But I would ask that we begin in this House to start talking about the real problems. We must begin a process of making sure that the committee of the House of Commons start to look seriously at what is involved in creating an income base program which will guarantee that Canadians, in whatever condition they find themselves at any point in time, will have an income at least sufficient to meet their daily requirements.
One might argue, and I can see the argument coming, how do we decide what are the basic daily requirements?
Hear, hear!
I can appreciate that the Hon. Member who applauded, the Hon. Member for-what is the riding?
That is all right; you just wander on.

I am not wandering on. I want to say that I can understand that someone as affluent as that Hon. Member from the Conservative Party would expect that his basic needs would be considerably higher than those, say, of the average New Democrat. I can understand, therefore, that the average Conservative would not want to share his ill-gotten gains with the balance of society.
Why do you not make a contribution yourself?

I can appreciate that Conservatives would want to have income-tested programs to make sure that people at the lower end were subjected to the humiliation of having to provide information about their day-to-day lives.
No one said that.
I can understand the Tory position.
You are dreaming again in technicolor.

I have lived through the Tory years. I know what the philosophy of the Conservative Party is. The Hon. Member who is interjecting is reinforcing on a daily basis that those who have hang on to what they have, and those who are in need, to hell with them.
That is your theory. That is what you practise.
That is the typical Tory attitude. I listened to the Hon. Member when he ran in the leadership contest of the Conservative Party. I saw through all of the smoke and mirrors-
I rise on a point of order.
-as he tried to appear as if he was in some way-

The Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) rises on a point of order.

June 22, 1984
Old Age Security Act
Mr. Speaker, let us use another day to discuss our political Parties. We are now talking about the disabled and the pensioners.

That was an interesting interjection. You are afraid to hear the truth, are you? However, as I was saying, I understand the Tory philosophy and I can appreciate that they do not want to see the kind of support base for the people I am talking about.
That is completely untrue and you know it.
I can well appreciate that they want to hold on to what they have, no matter how they got it, and share it with no one.
That is complete baloney!

It has always been the case. I do not deny for one moment, Mr. Speaker, right on that point, that if those Hon. Members came across a poor person on the street who should be benefiting from one program or another, they would be the first people to put their hands in their pockets and hand that individual a dollar. I do not deny that for a moment because they believe in the charity approach. They believe that if they give that poor person something, that person should be grateful forever.
Baloney!

What they do not seem to understand is that that poor person they meet on the street is but one of thousands, if not one of tens of thousands, of people who are facing similar kinds of problems. It is to that larger group that we are speaking today. We all want individual generosity but what we want more is to have people with an income by right, and an adequate income at that. I know it is foreign to the Tory philosophy to propose something like that, or even to listen to it. If they want to get up and tell us that somehow they will bring forward these programs, why have they not done so? I just find it offensive to listen to them.
However, let me say in conclusion that this particular proposal will pass because it does begin to address one particular small problem. But the real and more fundamental problem is one of basic income maintenance. Until we address that problem in a satisfactory and adequate way, we will be forever faced with piecemeal legislation which will never satisfy the basic needs of the majority of retired or unfortunate Canadians.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was interested as always in the Hon. Member's speech. I listened to him very carefully. He was talking about a guaranteed annual income, which has a great deal of attractiveness and it is something we should be
looking at very carefully. Later in his speech he said, in response to comments from the Conservative Party, that the Conservatives would like to see everything means-tested.
No way.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am just repeating what the Hon. Member said. He said that means testing was demeaning and it is not the way that we should be going. Is he not aware that a guaranteed annual income is the ultimate means-tested form of income security? It is given to people so that everyone has a minimum and it is phased out beyond that point on the basis of a means test. You cannot have a universal guaranteed annual income where everyone gets exactly the same amount regardless of their need. The purpose of a guaranteed annual income is to give it only to those who have the need, and it is phased out for income above that. There is a fundamental inconsistency in what the Hon. Member said. A guaranteed annual income is the antithesis of universality.
I disagree with the Hon. Member. We, of course, disagree on a number of technical points and on this one I disagree again.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: You cannot disagree with that.
You can. If you had a universally applied guaranteed annual income, you establish a tax base that will allow you to tax back from those who are in excess-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: So then it is not universal.
Of course it is universal.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Universal in the front row, selective in the back row.

No, it is absolutely universal. I think the Hon. Member would agree with me that, although he may not find it a satisfactory way of dealing with it, it is a practical approach to the problem he raises.

speechtext: Debate.

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to delay the debate. There are just three points I want to raise. I would like to remind the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) that the socialists of Canada do not have any monopoly on compassion, love or sharing.
That is right.
I take objection to any Member imputing motives to members of any other Party. He claims we do not have compassion.

I did not say that.
June 22, 1984

Our record will show that we have. However, I am not going to deal with that now. The Hon. Member is fully qualified to speak on socialism but he certainly does not know much about the PC Party or free enterprise.
One of the two main points I got up to speak on today is the Canada Pension. It is a splendid thing, but there are a number of people who never had the opportunity of contributing to the Canada Pension Plan. Consequently, when they reach the age of 55, 60 or 63, particularly if they are ill, they have no access to that fund. Many years ago we had pensions like the disability pension or the widows' pension. They have gone by the board and now we have the Canada Pension. It is a sad indictment of our society today that we leave a group of people without access to anything other than welfare when they reach the senior years of their lives. I think it behooves every government to look at this problem very carefully and come up with some solutions.
I am sure that every one of us here has had people come to us who, at age 55 or 60, have a sudden sickness and can no longer work. They are used to a reasonable standard of living. They are hard workers. Some of these people have looked after a widowed mother or a crippled father and so on. We do not need to go into all the causes, but there are people in that category and they have applied for the Canada Pension. They have to be told that we cannot pay them because they have never contributed. Well, they never had the opportunity to contribute. I hope we can deal with that problem because I find it very heartbreaking.
Another part of that question concerns the person who, because of sickness, has had to apply prematurely for the Canada Pension. They have not yet reached the age of 65. It takes too long, six to nine months, to process the application. This is a period of anxiety for these people. I would like to suggest to the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary that we endeavour to cut that time down to some degree.
The second reason I wanted to speak on this motion has to do with the misunderstanding about workmen's compensation. When a person is injured on the job and is no longer able to work, he gets compensation. During the period he is off work, that compensation is replacement of wages. He gets two-thirds or three-quarters of his wages and sometimes the employer provides the rest. Those are wages, but that is not what we are talking about. We are talking about those who have a permanent injury. They lost a hand and will never get it back. They are not on ordinary compensation; they are on what is called a temporary, partial disability, or they lose both legs and are on a permament total disability. The payment received is compensation for losing part of their body. I want to emphasize that difference. The compensation should not be included in wages.
It is so sad to see that some people who are getting the $50 increase this year are actually going to end up with less money than they had before. That is sad and it surely was never intended. I am sorry the Government has not brought in an amendment to cover this, because it was outlined very carefully by the Hon. Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday) and several others. I raised it personally with the Minister of Consumer
Old Age Security Act
and Corporate Affairs (Mrs. Erola) and she was going to take it up with the responsible Minister. The Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall) raised it on the floor of this House at least twice, and he indicated that he raised it in caucus also. I hope the Government will give this matter further consideration because it is utterly unfair for these people to get less money, when they have been promised an increase because of a sudden change in the rules and these payments are considered as wages. They are not wages and they should not be considered as wages.

I have a very brief question just to clear up a point. I do not believe the Hon. Member thought that I said that Conservatives did not have compassion. It was the opposite. I said that I did not doubt for a moment that Conservative Members had compassion.
However, that was not the issue. I said that I did not doubt for a moment that they would be the first to put their hand in their pocket to give some poor person $1 or $5 or $10. That is not the issue either. The problem is the tens of thousands of people you do not meet who are in dire need. Obviously you cannot reach into your pocket for all of them. That was the only point I made with regard to compassion. I think they are Neanderthal but I do not think they have no compassion.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether that requires an answer. However, we were not discussing handing money out of our pockets to people. We were talking about pensions for disabled people, old people and people in general. That is what we were talking about, not handing money out of our pockets because we feel sorry for someone.

speakeroldname: Mr. Russell MacLellan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) for his comments. I certainly appreciate the Hon. Member's sincerity in the remarks that he has made, as I appreciate the sincerity of his colleague, the Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday).
I would like to take exception though to the comment made that the Government is not tremendously concerned about the question of pensions. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) first outlined the federal Government's major objectives for

June 22, 1984
Old Age Security Act
pension reform in 1979,1 wonder how many of us realized how difficult this question would be and how much research and questioning would have to be done on this subject. The first thing which was done was to look at the system in place and discover why it was not working. This was done through a number of studies, including those by the Economic Council of Canada, the task force on retirement policy and the special Senate committee's report, Retirement Without Tears. Next came the national pensions conference in the spring of 1981.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I apologize for interrupting the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary at this time. I must inquire of him whether he is closing debate on second reading on behalf of the Minister.

speechtext: Third reading, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Included in the national pensions conference were representatives from the federal Government, provincial governments, private sector pensions employees, employers, women's groups and other individuals who were interested in this question from across the country. All of these groups continue to play an important role in the reform process and will continue to do so.
After the national pensions conference, work quickened on this subject and many groups came out with specific proposals. These proposals were very carefully studied. In December of 1982 we released a green paper that outlined these options and proposals which we felt needed further feedback. The parliamentary task force on pension reform was formed as a result of this green paper. After several months of public and private hearings the task force reported and two months later the federal Government, via the February, 1984 budget, outlined its strategy for reforming Canada's retirement income system.
While this is a very sketchy history of what has been done since 1979, I think Hon. Members will agree that it shows just how thoroughly pension reform has been studied. We have studied this subject well and I agree that at the present time we must implement some of the recommendations which came from this very important study. Bill C-40 is evidence of the period of study. As Hon. Members know, during the study period just past, a great deal of effort was directed to the various pension arrangements available to Canadians on retirement. The emphasis was on improving pension vehicles so that when an individual retires he or she will have a standard of living not unlike that enjoyed prior to his or her retirement.
The problems and concerns of pensioners within this retirement income system have not been forgotten. That is what we want to deal with through these amendments to the Old Age Security Act. We are not saying that we have a panacea for all questions within the retirement income system. It is for a specific purpose that we do not say that. The reason is that the subject is so detailed and has so many ramifications that we cannot possibly deal with this whole question in this particular Bill. We are saying that there is a very definite need among
pensioners, particularly single pensioners in the country. We must deal with this question as soon as possible.
The Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) says that the Government should be doing more on this question. He says that we should be looking at other aspects of the retirement income system. That is a very accurate statement but very much a simplification of the problem and the question. I sat with the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) in committee on the security Bill. In my opinion that Bill was literally filibustered by the Hon. Member. If the Hon. Member is serious about dealing with these questions, he must realize that these questions have to be dealt with as quickly as possible.
With regard to the record of certain Opposition Members in the very recent past, if we are going to tie up Bills the way Bills have recently been tied up-and I refer to the security Bill specifically-these important specifications are not going to be brought into law and made available to the very people who need them.
The guaranteed income supplement benefit was first introduced in 1967. It has been increased specifically by the Liberal Government since that time. Work toward the level of income that is needed in the country has taken place. Single pensioners received a full $20 increase as the first increase in 1969. Under the GIS program in 1980 single pensioners received an additional $35 increase. Married pensioners each received $17.50.
The proposals contained in this Bill will ensure that the two groups of pensioners that are not yet guaranteed a sufficient income under the Old Age Security Program, that is single and partial pensioners, will receive the increases they require. The first major proposal contained in Bill C-40 is the $50 increase for all pensioners getting what we call the single rate guaranteed income supplement. That includes GIS pensioners who are single, widowed, divorced and separated, as well as one-pension couples where one spouse is an Old Age Security pensioners and the other spouse is under the age of 60 and therefore does not yet qualify for spouse's allowance.
The $50 increase also goes to the spouse's allowance recipients who have been widowed and are now living alone. This increase will be made in two stages. The first $25 payment will be made next month and the second in December. These increases will, of course, be over and above the regular quarterly cost of living increases. In total, $50 in increases to the GIS single rate will be made. By December of this year single pensioners will be guaranteed 62 per cent of the income guaranteed to two-pension couples through the GIS and OAS programs.
The Hon. Member for Oxford stated that the OAS has been reduced from 20 per cent of the average industrial wage since its inception to 14 per cent of the average industrial wage. That is an accurate statistic. While we on this side of the House support the universality of programs such as Old Age Security, such a statistic demonstrates the need to pay particu-
June 22, 1984

lar attention to certain areas. Although we believe in universality for assistance to pensioners, should the funds that we have available be distributed to all pensioners to bring them from 14 per cent to 20 per cent of the OAS, or should we pay particular attention to pensioners in need through the GIS? With due respect to the Elon. Member for Oxford, I believe the funds would be better targeted toward the GIS for those people in particular need.
Appropximately 750,000 people will receive the $50 and approximately 25,000 more pensioners will qualify for the GIS for the first time as a result of the higher benefits under the GIS program. Hon. Members will know that this helps a segment of our population that is particularly in need.
The Hon. Member for Bow River talked about the needs of single women. Of this group who will receive benefits according to this Bill, 73 per cent are women. This is particularly important, as the Hon. Member for Bow River pointed out, because the majority of people living below the poverty line are single women. These are women who have spent a lifetime working in the home and in the community without access to the various work-related pension plans that are available to members of the workforce. Their only access to a pension plan is usually indirectly through their spouse. Quite often, these women are ultimately alone in retirement without the benefit of their spouse's pension plan.
Special emphasis on the problems facing women has been evident throughout the whole pension reform process. Today, the Government is taking a very important first step toward alleviating these problems. It is a first step because the $50 GIS increase has not solved the pension problems of all women. The Government fully recognizes that this increase is a short-term, even stop-gap measure to deal with an immediate concern, which is the well-being of today's elderly women and men who stand little, if anything, to gain from the reform of other aspects of our pensions system.
The partial Old Age Security pensioner is another group who have not yet been guaranteed a sufficient level of retirement income. They will receive the required increases as a result of other major amendments in this Bill. This will be accomplished by adding a flexible element to the GIS paid to partial pensioners. We will ensure that these pensioners will have access to the same total income as that provided to full pensioners through the OAS and GIS programs.
For example, according to the provisions of the Act, a pensioner who is entitled to only one-quarter of the basic Old Age Security pension is entitled to the same level of GIS as is provided to full pensioners. According to the proposals contained in this Bill, That pensioner will have access to the GIS benefit that is equal to the maximum benefit guaranteed to full pensioners, plus an amount equal to three-quarters of the OAS pension.
The Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) stated that even the inequitable treatment of one Canadian is worthy of the Government's attention. I agree with him. Some of the provisions in this Bill are particularly geared toward addressing the specific needs of some Canadians. For example,
Old Age Security Act
according to the present Act, Canadians can only apply for Old Age Security one year retroactively. According to this Bill, that period of retroactive application will be increased to five years. It is estimated that this only applies to approximately 50 people per year who do not apply for Old Age Security within a year after reaching the age of 65. Therefore this provision is very important to those 50 people.
Incidentally, I believe a partial reason why there are only 50 people who do not apply is that the Department is very efficient in giving notice to people approaching the age 65 to ensure they apply for their earned right. It is an earned right, as Members opposite have pointed out, because these people have built this country. We owe them for what they have done for the country during their working lives as homemakers or people in the workforce.
In the time I have remaining, let me deal with some of the questions that have been raised by Members at this stage of the debate. The Hon. Member for Oxford spoke of the workmen's compensation problem, as did the Hon. Member for Bow River and the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain. Unfortunately, a provision implemented in a finance Bill means that workmen's compensation benefits have now been deemed to be included in income. This is not something that the Government can ignore and it is currently studying it very carefully. However, it is not a matter which can be dealt with in this Bill.
Hon. Members have also mentioned the poverty line. We must consider the poverty line in the context of the whole question of income and the needs of senior citizens. As I said, the increases in the GIS payments will bring single pensioners to within 62 per cent of the incomes of married pensioners in this country. I think that is a significant statistic.
The general needs of pensioners are an ongoing question. It has been stated that the Government should have introduced this Bill earlier and that third reading should have taken place before now. That is completely irrelevant. It does not hold any credence at all. The first increase under this amended Bill will be due in July. Whether the Bill were passed February 29 or whether it will be passed June 30 is of no consequence. The importance is that it is passed in time for our senior citizens to receive the increases they so richly deserve.
I find that this is a tremendously important piece of legislation, and that has been recognized by the co-operation all Members of the House have given to its passage.
