speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation
speechtext: that the Bill be read the third time and do pass.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words in connection with third reading of Bill C-37. May I also express with regret that our critic, the Hon. Member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), is unable to be here. I want to express regrets on his behalf.
Let me say that I hope at least the gist of the amendments might be included in the regulations. The Hon. Minister I believe is prepared to take a careful look at them, and I appreciate that very much.
For a few moments now I would like to deal with third reading of this Bill, a very important Bill. We should cover a few points. First, what is the Bill going to do? It introduces something new as far as legislation in Canada is concerned, at least as far as the federal Government is concerned, and that is to provide a mortgage rate protection plan, which we refer to as MRPP. This was mentioned by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) in his Budget. We have been waiting for it, as have a great number of people.
The MRPP is an attempt to protect mortgagors from unaffordable increases in their interest rates, and as such, this has merit. The program is supposed to pay for itself. The Minister expressed the hope that no general revenue would be required to handle it. The premium is 1.5 per cent of the principal, and the highest principal permitted is $70,000 of the mortgage debt, or the face value of the mortgage, whichever is less. There is no repayment for the first two percentage points; there is a 2 per cent deductible, after which the program will pick up 75 per cent of the increase to an additional 10 percentage points. There is no protection at all beyond an increase of 10 percentage points.
I think it is important to make note of those items as well, as another one to which I will make reference. I am referring to the reference rate or the reference point which was discussed in committee. Many people will think that at whatever rate their mortgages are established, even if they are below the market value at the time, that the two percentage points start at that point. Of course that is not so. The program refers to a reference rate, and I would like to read into the record the information given to the committee in connection with that, so that the people who are following this debate with the idea of taking advantage of the program will not be under any misapprehension. Page 6:38 of the committee report reads:
This reference rate will be established by talcing the five major lenders on the market and taking the median of these five rates at any given time. So today, for example, the five-year term may be something of the order of probably 14.5 per cent. Let us say that five years from now, just for the sake of illustration, it is 19.5 per cent on that day. So then we will say that the reference rate has grown from 14.5 per cent to 19.5 per cent.
There is another statement which I think should be read. It appears on page 6:40 of the same report and reads:
June 22, 1984

The 5 per cent it goes up will be covered provided it is not only yours which goes up 5 per cent; it is the market which has gone up 5 per cent in that interval we are talking about.
The reference point should be taken into consideration.
A number of points have been raised about the MRPP which do not bear repeating. They were mentioned at second reading. However, I want to indicate that the Progressive Conservative Party is very concerned about the Canadian housing industry. We feel that Canada needs a housing program which will meet the needs to the greatest possible degree of all people. Of course that is easier said than done. We feel that there should be a multiple number of programs because home ownership is distinctive to our way of life. We think everyone possible should have the opportunity to own homes. It should be feasible for as many people as possible to own homes. This particular mortgage protection plan will not enable the housing industry to start meeting all needs. It will provide only one item of protection that may benefit a number of people.
Of course a great many people are concerned and interested in it. The document given to us in committee by the Minister's Department indicated the amount of interest evident at that point throughout Canada. It gave the number of telephone calls and written requests following the address of the Minister of Finance. The total accumulated telephone calls and written requests according to that document amounted to 5,161, most of which were from the Province of Quebec with 1,197 inquiries. My own province had 357. The second highest was the Province of Nova Scotia with 698, followed by British Columbia with 569. It is interesting to note that Yukon had none, but every province had some interest in the program. We have to conclude that a number of people are interested in it.
It behooves those people to check very carefully the premium payable for the life of the mortgage. It is not a one-year premium. It could amount to $1,050 on a $70,000 mortgage. They have to weigh the chance of interest rates rising more than the 2 per cent deductible and whether they will go up high enough to cover the increased interest as well as their premiums. They may actually be better off to use the premium of $1,050, or whatever it happens to be, to reduce the principal or their over-all mortgage. Surely the objective of everyone with a mortgage is to reduce it and eliminate it entirely as rapidly as possible. It will be a responsibility of the people themselves to look carefully at the provisions of the program. This Bill gives them the opportunity to purchase protection if they think it might be needed.
Had such a program been in effect in the last 10 years, there were very few occasions when it would have provided protection. Of course it would have provided gigantic protection in 1980 when interest rates rose from 14 per cent to 21.4 per cent. It would have provided tremendous protection during that period, but over the last 10 years or so there would not have been any particular advantage to a protection program. Of course, when people take out fire insurance they do not know whether their houses will burn down. They hope they will not, but they are purchasing protection in case they do. It
National Housing Act
may be that many people will be interested in coverage from that point of view as the interest rate is very unstable. It may rise significantly or not very much. We are all hoping that it will go down, not up.
If a person takes out this protection policy and the rate goes down, he is simply out the premium and would argue that it would have been better to reduce the principal on the mortgage rather than take out the policy. It will be up to people to decide in light of their own circumstances and the interest situation across the country.
Also the Bill deals with mortgage and home ownership security. The Government has indicated that there is a feeling that longer term mortgages should be available, for example, that mortgages should be renewed every 10 years instead of every five years. It feels that would contribute to the stability and growth of the building industry. It may. However, I would question going into a longer term mortgage unless I was fairly sure that the interest rates would keep rising. Over a 10-year period there is a great chance of interest rates falling as well, and one could end up stuck with a longer term mortgage. A large number of people lost their homes in 1980 and 1981 because they could not meet the costs of their mortgages as a result of large increases in rates of interest. While there are arguments on both sides for longer term mortgages, I am inclined to think that they might give stability to the building industry, but I am not so sure they will give any particular benefit to the rank and file.
I should like to deal for a moment or so with another aspect of the legislation. People certainly want the opportunity to own homes. However, many people across the country have reached the conclusion that they will never be able to purchase homes. For example, I spoke with a young married couple who have a son. They have given up all hope. This man works steadily, as does his wife. They have no hope of raising the down payment for a home. That is sad, but they reconciled themselves to that fact. They would like some security in renting, and we must give careful consideration to rental security.
The other day I received a letter from a constituent. He had been renting the same apartment for over ten years. The apartment building has been sold and he has been given his walking papers. That will disturb his whole life and that of his family. He thought he had security. We have to look at every angle of rental accommodation so that it meets the housing needs of our people. If they cannot have a home, rental is the next best thing.
There are a number of rental programs. I will just deal with one of them, co-op housing. I have an interest in this. I know people in the Calgary area who are very happy to be in a co-op housing project. It gives them security. They have a house, social life, and are happy with the amount of rent. Their rent is not subject to all the fluctuations that occur in normal renting.
If I owned an apartment, I could well increase the rent and still be competitive. I may want to charge all the market can bear. On the other hand I could be compassionate and charge

June 22, 1984
National Housing Act
the lowest rent possible. The rent in co-op housing is only affected by increased expenses. The co-ops have a democratic organization to run their projects. If there is an increase in taxes, the rent is increased to cover just that amount. It is not increased to provide a profit. If there is an increase in the insurance cost or other expenses over which they have no control, cognizance is taken of that and it is dealt with. That is one of the big advantages.
Something I like about co-operative housing is that it meets the needs of those who need it most. I made a check on this at a meeting I attended in Toronto. I wish to put on record how their wages relate to co-operative housing: 18.4 per cent had an annual income of less than $5,000, which is very low, at the poverty level; 52 per cent had an income of less than $10,000 a year, not a very high amount; 12 per cent had an income of $15,000 or less. That means that 82 per cent of those in the housing project had a salary of less than $15,000. They had a home, security, and a social life. They can run their own affairs. The others earned above that: 2.5 per cent with an income of less than $25,000, and 3.4 per cent with an income of more than $25,000.
People in almost every wage bracket live in the project. There is no social stigma if one person earns $5,000 and his neighbour earns $25,000. That is something I like about it. In building the houses, the construction industry benefits. The building of 10,000 units creates 16,000 jobs. That is what normally happens. There are a number of advantages to such a project.
There are other types of rental accommodation that I will not mention. We should look carefully at the building of new houses to see what benefits they provide, particularly for those who need it most, those with lower incomes. We should spend a good bit of time and provide a good bit of money in this area. We should increase that type of rental accommodation. That is very important. Many times subsidies to landlords do not help with rental costs. They do not produce one new house. That is the sad part about many of those programs. Money provided to co-operative housing projects produces new homes as well as the other advantages I mentioned. That is an important aspect of housing.
The third item covered in this Bill is very close to my heart, the rural and native housing program. This program does a tremendous amount of good. I recently referred a widow in my constituency to this program. She did not know what to do. Her roof was leaking, and she needed new windows and doors. This woman had two children. She was working but did not have enough income to repair her house. She did not want to give it up. Her husband had paid for it before he passed away. She cannot borrow money. The RRAP Program covers that need. She can get much of this work done. Some of it she will pay back, and some of it will be forgiveable.
This program is of tremendous advantage for such people who needs their homes rehabilitated, something all houses need sooner or later. I like this program very much. It was questioned to some degree in committee. In committee we received a lot of information about the number of people who
benefit from it. I will not deal with that. The program is applicable both to those on reserves and those in rural areas. A good percentage of the money is spent in both places.
There are three reserves in my constituency. I visit them periodically. They require more housing. Those that have been built are excellent. You have to be proud of them. When a family moves into such a house, it is like entering a new era. It brings happiness and satisfaction not only to those who live there but to everyone who sees it. Others on the reserve want this type of housing as well.
This program does a tremendous amount of good. If there were nothing else in this Bill other than the rural and native housing program, I would support it. The members of the New Democratic Party say they are going to oppose the Bill. Maybe they will have a change of heart. I hope so. I know the need on our reserves for new housing and the rehabilitation of present housing.
I know the need in rural areas. The Drumheller Valley was once a rich coal mining area. The mines have closed. Miners are not noted for building wonderful houses. The inside of their homes is better than the outside. The widows of those miners have been left with those homes. They are nice inside, but the windows do not keep out the cold. Storm windows and other things are required to make that house the kind of house that can stand weather with temperatures of 20 degrees below zero and 40 degrees below zero. This program is an excellent one and I would like to commend the Minister for continuing it.
He is now going to continue the program unilaterally. I think that is a good idea too. We asked the Minister in committee if the provinces would still be able to contribute if they wish. The answer was yes. We are getting the best of both worlds. Those of us who live in provinces in which the provincial governments want to contribute get 25 per cent more added to the total. No province will lose. The provinces can gain by joining the program, but if they do not wish to join, they then exercise their freedom of choice. That part of the Bill is, as well, an excellent part.
Canada needs about 210,000 housing units every year. We have not been meeting that need, but every old house that is made habitable goes toward meeting the housing need. Many people do not wish to leave the houses in which their children were born, or the houses in which their husbands or wives passed away. Those homes form a part of their entire being. This Bill enables them to keep their homes right up until the time they are no longer able to look after themselves.
As the Hon. Member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) said, we are supporting this Bill. I could go into a great deal of detail about housing but I will not do that today. I hope there will be other opportunities to do so. I will simply close by saying that we in the Progressive Conservative Party were somewhat disappointed with the Bill. First, we think it should have included some kind of tax credit program which would enable people who are otherwise unable to buy homes to do so. We
June 22, 1984

would like to see the building of a greater variety of homes. We would like to see the building of a greater variety of rental homes so that those who cannot buy a home can live in a good home. We would like to see all those things, but I suppose we cannot do everything at once.
We are somewhat disappointed with this Bill, but we are going to support it because it does give people an opportunity to protect themselves in some adverse circumstances if the interest rate rises. It will enable people to consider longer mortgages, which will perhaps have some benefit to the industry upon which we depend to build new houses. Finally, it extends the funding available to the rural and native housing program, and I think that that is excellent. We plan to support this Bill on third reading.

Mr. Speaker, the Bill has already been debated at second reading, has gone through committee, and has been studied in detail. The Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) has discussed the various component parts of the legislation, the only problem I have with the legislation is with that part which deals with the mortgage insurance plan. The balance of the legislation is supportable, although perhaps inadequate.
Unfortunately the mortgage insurance program is not, in my judgment, a particularly good proposal. It does not go to the heart of the problem. The heart of the problem is not the insurability of mortgage increases but the fact that mortgage rates have now reached the point where a significantly large proportion of the total population is excluded from home ownership, the events of the last two or three days alone have excluded something in the order of another 100,000 renters, who previously had the option of purchasing a home, from being able to qualify for mortgages at the current rate. This Bill does nothing about that. Those are the fundamental problems related to home ownership. The capacity to insure oneself against usurious increases does not solve that problem.
Quite bluntly, I do not like this approach to the problem. I do not think this is how we should deal with what has become a cancer in our society, the apparent right of individuals to gouge others. That is what has happened in the mortgage field. When mortgage interest rates rose to 21 per cent some 20 months ago, there was not one single person in the House who did not feel that something had to be done to separate mortgage interest rates from all other interest rates and recognize the absolute necessity for the funding of affordable accommodation. This Bill does not do that.
The only redeeming feature of this proposed legislation as it deals with mortgage insurance is that the program is voluntary. I suppose if people want to spend something in excess of $1,000 to buy themselves protection, then all I can say is I think they are being gypped and are making a mistake. Perhaps they should protect themselves some other way. Perhaps they should reduce their mortgages, or put their money in a bond, or do something as productive, rather than handing it over and finding that in the long run they will receive virtually, if not totally, no benefit from it.
National Housing Act
We know that mortgage interest rates would have to rise by 4.2 per cent before the people who had paid $1,000 out of their pockets would receive any benefit, taking into account the interest value on that money or the direct benefit they would receive if they reduced their mortgages by that amount. Taking those factors into account, mortgage rates would have to rise by 4.2 per cent before they would receive one single penny of benefit. They have to pay 1.5 per cent on the premium and do not receive anything for increases of another 2 per cent. They then receive the benefit of a reduction of three-quarters of 1 per cent for the next full point of increase. Even at that there is no guarantee that the calculation will be based upon their current mortgage interest rate since the Government has come up with some magic number called the reference rate.
All I can do in the time available to me is to say to the people: "For heaven's sake, be careful." To anyone who is listening today, or who might read Hansard, I say: "Be careful. Do not spend your hard earned money on this. It will not satisfy you, it will not protect you, it will not solve the problem of interest rates." In my judgment this program may in fact contribute to the interest rate difficulties, because the financial institutions will now feel less pressure as a result of the availability of an insurance program. The financial institutions will not feel compelled to work as actively as they might otherwise have worked to hold interest rates down.
From my point of view the main point of this exercise is to recognize that if interest rates for mortgages go from 14 per cent-and they are now in the environs of 14 per cent-to 18 per cent or 19 per cent, then the whole damned economy will be in a mess. If we allow that rise in interest rates to happen, then the problems of unemployment, domestic production, and domestic consumption, will be problems that will have to be faced by the House of Commons. If interest rates ever rise to a point where the purchase of this insurance would benefit anyone, then it is pretty clear to me that that rise in interest rates by itself will have triggered so many other problems in society that the end result will be a deterioration of Canada's economy.
The Minister knows my feelings on this matter. I have told him about them privately, and I have told him about them publicly. Without taking up a lot of time, I would therefore say to the Minister again: "I do not like it." In my judgment this program may exacerbate rather than solve the problem of mortgage interest rates.
I do believe it will become necessary, if not for this Parliament then for some subsequent Parliament, to devise new ways of funding mortgages in order to ensure that people will be able to acquire homes while retaining some sense of stability about repayment and the degree to which they have indebted themselves. I think that that will inevitably have to come to pass, and when it does then this program will be of absolutely no use.
Having said that, I am prepared to say that I do not disagree with the balance of the Bill. I found some little wrinkles in it of which I was not particularly fond, and I do

June 22, 1984
National Housing Act
worry about the capacity of the owner in some instances to benefit from the tax dollars that are apportioned for repairs and improvements to properties which otherwise might be uninhabitable. In my opinion that might encourage certain absentee landlords to deal improperly with their properties, to let them run down and to use access to government funding to offset their own obligations. However, it will, by virtue of the fact that it can be made available to the tenant, improve the living standards of the individuals in the homes. I suppose that is a benefit. I am prepared to live with that.
I would vote against the Bill because of the mortgage insurance program, but quite clearly I will not do that because it does not make much sense. I just hope that people who might be encouraged to buy into the program will heed my words, look at it carefully and come to the conclusion, as I have, that it might not help them. I hope they will decide to do something else with their hard-earned cash. If they choose to buy in, then I hope to God they will not receive any benefit from it because, if they do, the rest of society will suffer intolerably high interest rates.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments with respect to Bill C-37. The Bill is designed to accomplish three major purposes, one of which is to provide some measure of mortgage relief to home owners. It is with respect to that aspect of the Bill that I will make my comments.
The Bill is designed not to be a give-away program because people are expected to pay for what they are getting. What they are getting is a lot less that I fear they may think they will be entitled to. For a fee of 1.5 per cent of the amount of the mortgage, the mortgagor is granted relief with respect to 75 per cent of mortgage rate increases above a level of 2 per cent that is really self-insured from the beginning, up to a maximum of 10 per cent in terms of increase. That 1.5 per cent of the principal part of the mortgage is limited to $70,000. I am quite convinced that the majority of the people in the country think that-given the figures which I have referred to-in the event there is an increase in the mortgage rate at renewal above the 2 per cent which is covered, 75 per cent of that increase will be covered by this plan. That may or may not be the case.
I say it may or may not be the case because of the provision of Clause 34.83. Through a very convoluted system of prescribing interest rates, the insurer or, in this case, the corporation, may indeed determine that when a mortgage on an individual's home is up for renewal, the interest rate that is normally charged in the marketplace is less than the interest rate charged by the mortgage at the time of renewal.
Let us assume that the prescribed rate, which is an average or determined rate by the corporation, is less than the rate which would be charged by the existing mortgagee. What is the position of the insured who has paid 1.5 per cent? It is very clear that he will not be entitled to be covered for 75 per cent of the increase over the initial 2 per cent up to a limit of 10 per
cent of the renewal rate, but rather 75 per cent of the prescribed rate which is in effect at that time after taking into account the initial 2 per cent self-insured amount. That may be a difference of a substantial nature, depending upon the circumstances at the time. I think the public should be aware of that fact and recognize that they are not necessarily getting what they believe they are getting.
What is the justification for these differences? The Government may well say that if the average rate in the trade is something which can be determined, then the mortgagor should in fact renew at the average rate. How can anyone know what circumstances will apply at the time the mortgage matures? It is not a simple matter for someone to say that there is half a percentage point that he can obtain it for elsewhere if he will only go out and obtain it.
If one goes to another mortgagee-another financial institution which will provide funds-it means the following-the retaining of the solicitor of the mortgagee to search the title for the property so that he may in fact certify by legal opinion to the new mortgagee that the mortgagor has good and unencumbered title to the property. How much does that cost? Once again it depends upon the amount of the mortgage. In these cases it is not inconceivable that the cost would be somewhere in the neighbourhood of $500 or $600.
What else is required? It may well be that the new mortgagee will say that he does not wish to accept an old survey which the former mortgagee was prepared to accept and that he wants to know that the building is situated upon the land on which he has taken the mortgage. What would a new survey cost? It too may cost $400 or $500. In addition it is necessary for the mortgagor to discharge the existing encumbrance. Once again, the preparation of the discharge documents- which are set by fee under a schedule in most provinces-will cost $50 or $75.
We are then told that the mortgagor should-for the half a percentage point which he will lose-go to the average mortgage lender and obtain the average rate of interest and not have this corporation, for the payment of his premium of 1.5 per cent, cover the actual-not the deemed or the assumed- rate of interest that is in effect in the country at the time that the mortgage comes up for renewal. It is obvious, by the time that individual pays $1,200 or $1,300 to change mortgages, that it is more appropriate for him to assume the loss personally that he would sustain as a consequence of buying this insurance which does not cover him for what he thinks it will cover him. There will be a great number of times when individuals with this kind of coverage will ultimately be confronted with this problem. That will happen as mortgages mature. People will come screaming to the Government, telling it that they did not get what they bargained for. It is the fine print that those people are not reading. It is the fine print which is not being advocated and publicized by the Government so that the people will know exactly what they are getting for what they are spending.
There is another matter which I would like to draw to the attention of the House. It arises as a consequence of the
June 22, 1984

provisions of Clause 34.85. The concept is that with this insurance-having paid 1.5 per cent of the principal amount of the mortgage-the mortgagor has an asset which can be assigned to a subsequent purchaser of the property. Or, so it seems.
If one examines the provisions of Section 34.85, one will notice under subparagraph (b) there is a provision for that assignment which reads as follows:
A contract entered into under subsection 34.82(1)
(b) may not be assigned on the part of the home owner, except to a person
(i)	who assumes all the liability of the home owner in relation to any base loan or protected loan outstanding ...
(ii)	who acquires the interest of the home owner in his principal residence, subject to any encumbrance securing the base loan or protected loan ...
There are two ways, in effect, which are covered specifically by this section. One is with an absolute assumption of liability, which very rarely, incidentally, Mr. Speaker, any purchaser of a home undertakes. In most circumstances there is no specific assumption in law; if you acquire the interest of the home owner and begin to make those mortgage payments you are one of the persons obliged to continue to make those payments. Without actually being on a covenant, you are one of the persons obliged to make the mortgage payments but there is very rarely any direct assumption of the mortgage loan.
Section 34.85(b)(ii) normally covers the situation where you simply buy the property subject to a mortgage and do not assume the obligations of the original mortgagor. The only trouble with that circumstance is that it applies to the principal residence. It may well be, Mr. Speaker, with respect to the way in which we have dealt with principal residences, that the purchase by the new owner is not of the principal residence. It may not be in fact the principal residence of the home owner at the time of the acquisition, because he may indeed have used it in the interim for some other purpose which destroys the principal residence concept. Accordingly, I draw that matter to the attention of the House as well because the full ability with respect to assignment may not in fact be as it appears on the surface of the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I would also like to take a few moments and discuss the mortgage protection plan under Bill C-37. I worry about this plan. I believe it gives the Canadian public some false hope that possibly there will be security in interest rates. But this Bill is not really accomplishing that and I can give you some statistics on it.
It will not help a person in a period of very low interest rates who at that time takes out a five-year mortgage-and that is only if the mortgage renewal happens to come at the right time. But if that person takes out his mortgage at an interest rate of between 10 per cent and 11 per cent and those rates soar up to 17 per cent or 18 per cent it will help. However, it is too costly for a person today to gamble with $1,050 which is in essence added to the principal of his mortgage. It costs too much. I believe it is too expensive and I do not feel it will work.
National Housing Act
If this Bill was to be effective it should have been brought in when interest rates were high, not when they started to decline.
I believe this Bill, as a solution to our housing problems today, fails Canada.
I know the Hon. Minister who is responsible for CMHC has a problem in these times. I know he is not in control of the economic situation in the country. However, the statistics on the housing industry show a very serious situation right now. I understand part of the reason for this situation, to which I am going to refer, is because of the grants given by both the Ontario Government and the federal Government last year.
When housing starts were down 27 per cent in the month of April, I started to worry. When housing starts are at 50 per cent of what they should be, I worry. One of our key responsibilities should be to encourage all Canadians to own homes. I believe the Minister agrees with me on that. I believe that the Minister is totally in agreement with home ownership, to as large an extent as possible.
There are several other statistics on housing which worry me as well. In 1983, home ownership dropped-and this will not sound like very much-to 62.4 per cent from 62.7 per cent in 1982. That is a downward trend, but that is not the trend that bothers me as much as the longer term trend. The percentage of all owner households in the country is now below what it was ten years ago. In trails 1963 levels by almost six percentage points. That is the period of time in which the Liberals have been in power. It proves to me that this Government has not identified this crisis and has not dealt with it. It has not put the proper incentives in place to solve the problem.
I feel that this Bill is not going to solve the problem. This is a patchwork bill, it is a band-aid bill. We have seen enough band-aid bills in this House. This Bill is not going to encourage home ownership so that we can even get back to the 1963 levels. I know the Minister would tell me that it is a different society today, there is greater mobility in the work force and people do not have the same interest in owning homes. Perhaps the Canadian psyche today is not to save money, but to spend it while we have it, but I feel very strongly that one of the prime interests we should have in this country is to create home ownership for every single person.
My constituents have called me about the mortgage protection plan. They have asked me what they should do. I have told them that at the present time I cannot recommend it. And I put it in a partisan way. I said to them, "There will be an election. I am certain that following the election a Conservative Government will come in. Because of our policies we will put stability into interest rates. We will not allow these large troughs and peaks which the Canadian people have had to suffer through".
I read in an article the other day that since 1977, $40.5 billion in equity funding has left this country. We then in turn go overseas to borrow debt capital to bring it back in. Part of the trouble in the housing industry is that the Government, which is trying to provide so many safety nets, has not paid attention to the average Canadian who wants to own a home, or to the farmer, many of whom, as the Minister of Agricul-

June 22, 1984
National Housing Act
ture (Mr. Whelan) knows, are in a very critical position. Many of them have over financed, which I will acknowledge, but those who have not, cannot afford to borrow money at even a 12 per cent interest rate and make a decent return on capital.
In essence this plan protects the homeowner for 75 per cent of an increase above 2 per cent. For example, someone takes out a one-year mortgage at 12.75 per cent and renews at 18 per cent. After deducting the $1,050 premium he would be saving only $431. I could not recommend to anyone spending $1,050 in order to receive $1,481 in return. 1 think that is bad business.
We are on the right track here, and I would like to see this given deep study. The idea is good. It is a beginning. I have not had enough time to really analyse it. It has to be looked at in a broader sense. Perhaps two or three years down the road when interest rates are at a reasonable level it will be to the advantage of the home owner. But at present, when mortgage rates are 13 per cent and 14 per cent, if they went up to 18 per cent there would not be much protection. The premium would be an additional burden in that critical first year.
We must have a committee to analyse housing in this country. We have to determine what we can do to get homeowners back to the 1963 level, which was in excess of 68 per cent. Everyone should own a home. Home construction is 100 per cent Canadian. They are manufactured here, the raw materials come from here, as do the finished products such as kitchen and washroom fixtures. Everything is made in Canada. If you doubled the number of homes being built this year you would create 230,000 jobs, given 2,300 jobs for every 1,000 homes. That would take a big chunk out of our unemployment figures.
The program of last year, even though I do not agree with grants, did work. It assisted people. I have to commend the Minister. I have had some difficult problems with those grants. Some have been marginal because of a question as to whether the foundations were in on time. I appreciate the co-operation the Minister has given me because it has assisted my constituents. For that I am grateful. The grant system worked last year in a recession, but possibly it will not work this year.
We should sit down and see what will work. I am afraid this program will not catch fire. I am afraid that if we pass this today, by the end of the year it will be as successful as the Sports Pool, which was a disaster. If this is in place when interest rates go down to-and I am dreaming now-8 per cent, then I would recommend that every home owner buy mortgage insurance. Possibly the problem is in the timing, but obviously if it is in place it may help in the future, as long as interest rates go down. But we must not underestimate the problem. How can interest rates go down when the Government borrows 92 per cent of our savings? That is not the Minister's fault, it is the fault of the entire Government. It is a problem brought upon this country after 21 years of Liberal rule.
I would like to conclude my remarks by saying that I will not support this Bill. I do not think it is right or that it has been well thought through. It should not be approved at this time because it is patchwork. It may fool the public but it cannot fool the actuaries or the Members of this House. It will not solve the problems we face. However, I have appreciated the opportunity of saying a few words on the Bill. I hope the Minister will continue to think about it and look for ways to improve the housing program to assist all Canadians to own their own homes.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to make a short intervention on this housing Bill. The only point I want to discuss is the mortgage insurance program. I want to associate myself completely with the remarks of the Hon. Member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell) and the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans).
In my view this mortgage insurance Bill is politically motivated. It is only a veneer so that the Liberal Party will be able to go out during the next election campaign and tell people it has done something to try and stabilize interest rates for those who are going to own their own homes. You have heard the figures given by the two Members I just mentioned. People in the insurance industry feel that the homeowner would be better off paying $1,000 off the principal amount of the mortgage rather than paying this premium for so little benefit.
I think to a certain degree that the Private Members' Bill I introduced a number of years ago is the reason that this sort of politically motivated Bill has been brought forward. At that time my Bill proposed that if people had paid a mortgage for a year they should be allowed out of the mortgage on payment of a three-month penalty. That is the situation in the United States and in the United Kingdom. However, the banking community in Canada was very upset about that. As a matter of fact, a few days after I introduced this Private Members' Bill I had a visit from the president of the Bankers' Association who thought it should be withdrawn.
But my proposal went to the real problem faced by people with mortgages at high interest rates. If they had taken a five-year mortgage at 18 per cent interest, for example, after one year they could have paid it off with a three-month penalty. If they went the full term the difference could be as much as $13,000 between what they might pay at interest rates as they were last winter compared to what they are now, around 12 per cent.
This Bill has been introduced to try to show the people that there is a concern by the Government and a sort of protection. In actual fact I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that very few Canadians will ever take advantage of this mortgage insurance plan. The reason is that you can try to bring forward good looking legislation, and you can dress it up, but the native intelligence of the people at large is such that they are not going to waste their money. Most of them are going to believe that they are wasting their money. If they reduce their principal by $ 1,000 each year over the period of time they are going
June 22, 1984

to save themselves an awful lot in interest payments. They are probably going to save themselves as much as they could gain by investing in a mortgage insurance protection program.
I really believe this is a politically motivated Bill designed to give the perception to the Canadian public that the Government is acting in their interest. All Parties are going to let it go through because no one wants to be perceived as being against something which is being dangled out. It is only cosmetic in nature. Other provisions in the Bill are more meaningful than this cosmetic provision. I think it is trying to pull the wool over the eyes of the Canadian public.
The interesting thing is that there is a small credit union in Prince Rupert, British Columbia which has been offering mortgage insurance at .5 of a percentage point rather than 1.5. If they have been able to do that for three years, why are we charging three times the premium? Having said that, there is no doubt that it is going to go through. It is not going to be used by anyone. The perception may be there but the Canadian public is going to be an awful lot wiser than the Government thinks. In the long run this is just going to be another useless statute on the books.

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBlanc (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will first thank the House for its courtesy. I was distracted and thought we were on second reading. I would like to make a few short comments.
National Housing Act
In response to the Member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell), under no circumstances have I indicated that this was a total solution to some of the longstanding housing problems, although I did put some statistics on the record in an answer to the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) yesterday which indicated that the picture may not be as dark as it seems. In fact there was an increase of 7 per cent in housing starts between April and May of the current year.
With regard to the question raised by the Opposition House Leader referring to an amendment requested by the Hon. Member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney), it was ruled out of order. But we were sympathetic to the substance of what was proposed. In fact, in the case of the mortgage protection plan, floating homes or that type of houseboat will be covered under the mortgage protection plan. The difficulty arose, and arises, when the mortgage insurance applying to floating homes is discussed, for the same reason that mobile homes at one time were not covered by mortgage insurance. Discussions with the industry and a willingness to try and find solutions brought forth some amendments which have worked.
The Hon. Member for Vancouver Centre forced us to focus on the issue more quickly than we might have liked. Although we were quite sympathetic to the substance, I am sure that it will come up again and we will continue to work and where possible, by regulation, try to find some acceptable solutions.
Some Hon. Members have referred to the mortgage protection plans as an innovation. Some have expressed doubts as to whether it will see heavy take-up in applications. Some have pointed out some of the limitations that it does contain. I do not think I should spend too much time quibbling with some of these opinions. It is innovation. In our examinations in other countries we have not found cases where this type of program is used, although in some countries we have found an insurance formula for people who were threatened with the loss of their homes because of the loss of a job or similar problems.
The legislation is voluntary and obliges no one to make a decision in this matter. My hope is very firm that over time we may find that there are some amendments which would bring considerable improvement. The mortgage protection program is a service to Canadian home owners who may be worried about possible increases in mortgage interest rates. It is addressed to people who are afraid that, when the time comes to renew their mortgage, interest rates may have risen so high that they will not be able to make the monthly payments. To these people it offers, for a fee, some help and protection to assure that any increases will be kept within their ability to pay.
I hope that it is clear, and I believe Hon. Members on both sides have said that it is not a subsidy program and is not designed to protect home owners against any increases, however small, in mortgage interest rates. It is not designed to shelter home owners from every shift in interest rates. Most Canadians who decide to invest in a home anticipate changes and are prepared to cope with them. During the interest rate crisis of a couple of years ago we saw that many Canadians were prepared to make rather considerable adjustments. The

June 22, 1984
National Housing Act
MRPP is intended to help with abnormal circumstances, with eventualities which we do not expect and which people may not be in a position to deal with.
There are other reasons as well, Mr. Speaker, why the plan includes risk sharing provisions such as the 2 per cent deductibility feature. It is important that the mortgage market, like other free markets, should remain competitive. As long as the home owner is going to have to share the cost of higher interest rates, he will shop for the best deal he can get when his mortgage comes up for renewal.
In that connection I would like to emphasize again that the mortgage plan is voluntary. If in their judgment it is not a wise investment, then obviously Canadians will make the judgment that they feel is right.
Although we dealt with the Bill rather quickly, I believe that the committee discussion was informative and useful. I think it went a long way to answering some of the hesitations that Hon. Members had.
I would like to thank Hon. Members for their support and their interest in that part of the Bill which deals with the rural and native housing programs which extend, for the first time, benefits to all parts of Canada. Perhaps I should indicate quickly what the changes are.
As Hon. Members will recall, the legislation as it is now requires that assistance to allow people in designated areas to acquire their own houses can be provided only if the cost is shared between the federal Government and the provinces. Some provinces dropped out of the program and one province never participated. Other provinces, while participating, made their assistance conditional on such terms and conditions that we felt they were inconsistent with the very objectives of the program.
Some Hon. Members have expressed regret that we have not achieved unanimity among all governments as to the objectives and methods of operation. I agree, it is regrettable. This divergence of opinion, however, cannot be allowed to deprive people of urgent need of shelter. That is why we are proposing that the funding and administration of the program can be assumed unilaterally by the federal Government. But those who wish to continue to participate will be welcome. In fact, as the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) indicated, it will be an additional contribution to that sector of the population which is very often most in need.
I appreciated the contributions made by all Hon. Members who expressed a sincere interest in the operation of this program and in the welfare of rural and native people who live in remote areas of the country. I believe that by enacting this Bill into law we will have given new life and strength to this vital and rather successful program. I am grateful that we have been able to move as we have with this legislation. Again, it is not a cure-all for all housing problems, but I think it goes some way and makes available to those who choose to avail themselves of it a form of insurance and a form of protection.
However, I suspect that over a period of time we will be back with some improving amendments.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me say first to the Minister that I appreciate his contribution on third reading. When the Minister is handing out tributes with respect to this matter I know he would want to say that we in the Official Opposition have been constructive. We have attempted to deal with legislation on the floor of the House in that manner, particularly with respect to this legislation.
He will appreciate that we find that there are considerable shortcomings. We have tried to point these out to the Minister, and have tried in many ways at committee stage and in the course of debate in the House to indicate to him that some of the initiatives fall far short of the mark. We rather take the position that when it comes to the question of mortgage interest protection, it is because of the Government's handling of the economy that we found ourselves in phenomenally high interest rate circumstances with a crushing burden on the home owners of Canada. Those have been the circumstances that have really precipitated this legislation.
Of course, I do not want to be partisan, but I remember the pronouncement of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) when he was in the opposition. Interest rates were at 13 per cent. I was a member of the Government of Canada at the time and a member of the Cabinet. I must admit that I had difficulty shaving in the morning when I contemplated interest rates of 13 per cent. I thought to myself that these were usurous levels of interest rates and that we must do what we can to bring them down. Of course, there was an election and the results are known. The new Government came in.
But when the President of the Treasury Board was in opposition and speaking with respect to financial matters, he made a statement that any person in political life with integrity who allowed interest rates to exceed 14 per cent had only one honourable course. That was to resign from any Cabinet which allowed that level of interest to rise above 14 per cent. I was impressed with the sincerity of the President of the Treasury Board when he said that, because I felt very strongly that as a Government we had to do what we could to keep interest rates low for the average home owner and businessman.
History is there for us to see. Interest rates skyrocketed to 22 per cent, a level that was described as being the level of interest rates which at one time would be charged to customers of organized crime who were rather untrustworthy. That was the prime rate for a long period during the time that the Government has been in power.
We need some form of protection for home owners when they are faced with having to renew mortgages, as we all are. I have a mortgage coming due on July 1. It is at 13 per cent. I was considering what to do, whether to have a mortgage of one or two years at 15 per cent, or perhaps of three years in excess
June 22, 1984

of 15 per cent. It is a lot of money for a humble working man like myself.
I say to the Minister that this particular response falls short of what we had hoped and expected in this country with respect to the problems we face with present high interest rates.
There are reasons why we have tried to deal with this Bill and put it through at this point in time. I will admit candidly that there is a political element to it. Our position is simply that this is the Government's best shot. This is the best it can do. This is as good as it will give us. As the Loyal Opposition, we are prepared to put the Bill through and tell the people of Canada that we in this Party are thinking about the horrendous problems that are created by high interest rates. We are thinking in terms of the policies and initiatives that can be taken by the Government of Canada which we hope to form after the next election. When we become the Government, I can assure the Minister and members on the government side that we will devote our attention and energies toward protecting home owners in a more significant way against the very ugly prospect that comes with high interest rates than has this Government.
We intend to do everything possible to make sure that home mortgage interest rates go down. I can tell the Minister that our Party is committed to protecting the average person in this country, the average home owner as well as the person who lives in rented accommodation. That is the basis upon which we in the Opposition allow this legislation to go forward. That is the basis upon which we say to the Minister that we have tried to do a responsible job in our consideration of this legislation. We find very significant shortcomings. While we wish the Minister all the best with this legislation and hope that it has some good effects, we say that it is far short of what the people of Canada should be able to expect. Accordingly, we will see the Bill passed by the House of Commons today so that it can be sent to the other place for consideration.

speechtext:
Just a second, Mr. Speaker, we want to hear the Parliamentary Secretary on second reading.
Mr. Ralph Ferguson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister
of Finance): In view of the very heavy work load, Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief.
The purpose of Bill S-14, passed by the Senate on June 6, is to implement the double taxation convention between Canada and the United States of America. The implementing legislation is found on pages 1 and 2 and the text of the convention together with its two amending protocols are found in schedules I, II and III, pages 3 to 64.
Canada-United States fiscal relations are governed by a tax treaty which was signed in 1942. It would be clear to everyone that a tax treaty that has not basically changed in 40 years needs to be modernized, even though it has been a useful instrument. The new convention, when in force, will replace the 1942 tax treaty.
The convention is a balanced instrument which addresses a broad range of issues and problems affecting a significant number of individuals and corporations on both sides of the border. It took some ten years to negotiate. Its ratification is eagerly awaited by those affected. The text of the proposed convention was made public on the date of its signature, September 26, 1980. Following its publication, a number of professional associations in the two countries commented extensively on its terms and pointed to a number of deficiencies. That, plus important changes in the U.S. legislation concerning the taxation of capital gains made it necessary to introduce some amendments to the original text. The first protocol was signed and published on June 14, 1983.
Finally, a change introduced in the U.S. concerning the taxation of social security benefits lead to the signature of a second protocol on March 28, 1984.
I shall now refer briefly to some of the provisions of the convention. It provides that the maximum rates of withholding taxes on non-residents may not exceed 10 per cent on direct dividends, patent royalties and technical know-how payments and 15 per cent on portfolio dividends, interest and periodic pension payments. Under the existing treaty, the withholding tax rates on non-residents are generally 15 per cent. Copyrights royalties and certain interest payments are exempt from the withholding tax.
Income or profits from immovable property, including natural resource royalties, may be fully taxed in the country where the property is situated. Gains arising on the disposition of certain property may also be fully taxed in the country where it is situated. In view of the fact that the treatment of capital gains represents a significant change from the existing convention, special rules are also included to avoid the disruptive effect of this change on investment existing at the time of signature of the convention.
The convention contains a number of other important provisions such as: the scope of the exemption for international transport profits is extended; social security benefits will be exempt in the country in which they arise and only half of their amount will be subject to tax in the country of residence of the recipient; the deduction for contributions by a resident of one country to a university or a charitable organization in the other country will be liberalized; special problems affecting border workers will be addressed; the two-year exemption for visiting teachers will be removed.
This listing is not intended to be comprehensive, but it gives an indication of a number of the issues dealt with in the convention.
The convention will enter into force only after it has been ratified. It will generally be applicable, for the withholding tax, on the first day of the second month following the date of ratification and, for other taxes, on the first day of January following the date of ratification. I have been informed that the United States is likely to be in a position to ratify the convention in the near future. It is important that Canada also be in that position soon, therefore I commend this bill to the favourable consideration of this house today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking on behalf of the Progressive Conservative Party and the Official Opposition to Bill S-14 which relates to the tax convention between Canada and the United States of America, I think it is important and highly desirable that we place on the record some general comments with respect to the processing of this legislation, and indeed this kind of legislation.
We have seen in the House of Commons in the last few days a demonstration of what we earnestly believe is parliamentary democracy, a duty of the Loyal Opposition to oppose the Government in that official way. Our responsibility under the British tradition in force in Canada since Confederation in
June 22, 1984

1867 is to examine with great care and diligence all the measures put before the House of Commons by the Government. In those cases where we think those measures may not be to the advantage of Canada and the citizens of Canada it is our bounden duty to raise the objections we can and bring to public attention those provisions which may have an adverse effect on Canada and Canadians.
That is what indeed the Opposition did with respect to Bill C-9 which was before this House and dealt with the Canadian Intelligence Security Service. The Opposition brought to the attention of Parliament, and through that parliamentary vehicle to the public, the faults of that Bill, the philosophy behind the Bill with which we have real disagreement. In that parliamentary exercise, I am sure we have cast a great deal of attention on that legislative measure, Bill C-9. If it appeared to be extreme in terms of parliamentary action, then we accept whatever responsibility we must assume for that action, because we thought and earnestly believed it was in the interests of all Canadians to focus attention on the legislation contained in Bill C-9 relating to the Canadian intelligence service.
We see quite the opposite attitude evidenced today in what I will say with respect to Bill S-14. We regard this Bill as the legitimate action of the Government of Canada in following the process which led to the adoption of a convention after agreement between the Government of Canada and the Government of the United States. We will co-operate, as we are now doing, to see that this Act of government receives proper attention and concurrence from the Parliament of Canada in such a way that it will benefit the taxpayers of Canada and indeed, incidentally and at the same time, the taxpayers of the United States of America.
My point is that we see our duty very clearly. Sometimes our duty is to oppose the Government to the bitter end. On other occasions our duty as opposition Members is to co-operate with the Government in order to achieve a benefit for the citizens of Canada, the people whom we represent in the Parliament of Canada. It is with that preface that I want to make some remarks about Bill S-14. It is with that thought in mind that what we are doing here in our function is co-operating in the way that we must in order to bring about what we are told is action beneficial to the people of Canada.
As has already been indicated, Bill S-14 simply is the authority from the Parliament of Canada to the Government of Canada to concur in and implement a convention between Canada and the United States of America with respect to taxation and the collection of taxes. In legislative terms, the Act itself is very simple. It contains only the necessary technical provisions. What is of wider importance is the convention itself which contains the operative provisions. As I have indicated already, we in the Opposition in these circumstance must rely upon the advice we receive from government, through its representatives in the House of Commons, in this case the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. MacLaren).
Tax Convention Act
As I understand it, the provisions were negotiated in good faith between representatives of the Government of Canada and representatives of the Government of the United States of America. For us to examine with a fine-tooth comb, or put under a parliamentary microscope, the provisions which have been agreed to between the representatives of those contracting parties would not be an appropriate response to the request to give concurrence to this legislative measure. In other words, it is not the function of Parliament to review what the officers of Canada and what the officers of the United States have in good faith consummated. However, at the same time we cannot simply absolve our duty or our responsibility to the people of Canada by saying that we are placing total reliance upon the officers whose responsibility and duty it was to construct this convention. We certainly have to give it some kind of review, and that is my purpose in speaking to Bill S-14 today.
The purpose of the convention, as we know in all such conventions in relation to taxation, is to avoid unfair treatment of taxpayers in the contracting states, in particular the unfairness of double taxation. In that respect of course we concur in the principle of avoiding double taxation, because it simply is unfair. It is unfair by definition. To the extent that the convention is approved by Bill S-14, of course we concur, but we are not certain that that is the only way the matter can be resolved. However, as I have already indicated, we are entitled to rely upon the advice given to us by the Government of Canada through the Minister of State for Finance.
Notwithstanding that we concur in the principle of avoiding double taxation between taxpayers of Canada and taxpayers of the United States, there are matters which should be recorded, as they will have a real effect upon Canadian and American taxpayers. Our concern is for the taxpayers of Canada we represent in the House of Commons and in the Parliament of Canada.
There are a number of matters to which I want to direct some specific remarks, but first I want to deal with the whole system of conventions between Canada and the United States. We have different systems. We both employ democratic systems of government in respect of which we are both proud. However, they are different systems. The United States of America has a presidential republican system of government. The power in that country is divided between the legislative body in the United States Congress and the executive represented by the duly-elected President of the United States.
The executive in the U.S. has negotiated a convention with Canada, but it requires the approval of Congress. As the Parliamentary Secretary indicated, approval of this specific convention relating to taxation has not yet been granted. That is a matter we have to take into account. Why do we have to take it into account? When we approve the legislation which enables the adoption of the convention by the Government of Canada we in Parliament have abrogated the power to do anything about this particular measure. We have left it up to the Government of Canada. We in Parliament have left other things up to the Government of Canada relying on the good

June 22, 1984
Tax Convention Act
faith and good judgment of the Government, and we have been very sorry that we allowed them that authority. But we recognize that with a majority in the House of Commons and with control of Parliament, the Government would do it in any event. However, that does not excuse us from raising a protest about legislation when danger signals occur.
I want to raise a danger signal with this process because we have been through it in other ways. I am quite serious in my statements in this regard. I have before me material with respect to what is of grave concern to myself, and particularly to people in Nova Scotia living in that part of the province called South Western Nova. It relates to Georges Bank. We are experiencing a certain amount of deja vu with this convention because the Government of Canada negotiated with the Government of the United States a convention with respect of fisheries rights in relation to Georges Bank, the most fertile fishing grounds in the world, upon which many Nova Scotian fishermen are totally dependent for their livelihood. The negotiations were conducted in good faith, as I am sure the negotiations with respect to the taxation treaty were conducted in good faith. The end result was that the Congress of the United States would not approve the convention. The matter was deliberated over a long period of time. The articles were formulated. The "i's" were dotted and the "t's" were crossed. It was negotiated and renegotiated, considered and reconsidered, viewed and reviewed. Finally the convention was formulated, but it was not approved by the Congress of the United States because a Senator from Rhode Island took a look at it and said that he did not agree with it, and that he did not think it was fair to U.S. fishermen on the East Coast. He decided that that convention ought not to be approved. There was not enough interest in the Congress of the United States to override the view and opinion of that particular Senator, and one or two others, one of whom was unfortunately that great guardian of civil rights in the United States, Senator Kennedy. A few of them got together and blocked consent and concurrence of the United States Senate to that treaty.
It is not a light matter when we in the Parliament of Canada just automatically give approval to a convention which has been negotiated by the Government of Canada with the Government of the United States, because we do not always get reciprocity on the other side; we do not always enjoy have the same response by the appropriate House in the United States Congress, as evidenced in the Georges Bank situation.
Because I think it is of vital importance, in that it involves the very livelihood of thousands of people in the Province of Nova Scotia, let me review briefly what happened as a result of the refusal of the United States Congress to approve the treaty and convention relating to fisheries rights on the Georges Bank. They are now before the International Court in the Hague. They are arguing like fishmongers literally before an international court of dubious jurisdiction over who will be allowed to harvest Georges Bank.
