speechtext: They have jurisdiction.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1984 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: There is the difference between a young lawyer and an old lawyer. I said dubious jurisdiction. The young lawyer apparently does not know that an international court has no inherent jurisdiction. Nobody gave it jurisdiction. There is no super power that formulates an international court and gives it jurisdiction.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1984 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: I have my Master's in international law.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1984 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
An international court only gains jurisdiction from the parties that come before the court. They can confer jurisdiction generally by a treaty, as the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) knows, or they can confer jurisdiction with respect to a particular case. In the case of the Georges Bank matter, jurisdiction was conferred by consent and concurrence for that specific case. The international court in the Hague has no right to intervene in disputes over Georges Bank and fishermen. That is why I used the term dubious jurisdiction. There is no basic inherent reason why the International Court in The Hague should be deciding a problem between fishermen from the eastern United States, the New England States, and from Southwestern Nova.
The only reason they are deciding that is because the Government of Canada, sitting in the national capital of Ottawa, and the Government of the United States, sitting in the national capital of Washington, have decided that that is the way to get rid of the problem, that that is the way to treat the fishermen of Nova Scotia and New England.
There is a group of lawyers like my friend from the New Democratic Party arguing over what are the essential, vital and important rights. They are talking about ancient history, legal documents and so on. They are not talking about people or about lives. They really do not care if the multimillion dollar scallop industry is lost to Nova Scotia. It is just a matter of charging fees. No doubt many lawyers are charging immense fees to handle this case. That does not bother the Hon. Member of the New Democratic Party. He is a lawyer. Like he says, he has a Master's degree in international law. He thinks that is the way these things should happen. I do not think that is the way things should happen. I think the future of the parties is largely dependent upon the determination of this dispute. They should be involved in it, not a bunch of lawyers in The Hague.
That is the problem with international conventions. When we cannot agree. All sorts of terrible and horrible things can happen. That is why we consider with a great deal of responsibility a measure like S-14. We do not want to end up in international courts over this kind of dispute. We do not want people in the State of Texas or the Province of Quebec to be burdened with excessive taxation because we cannot come to some kind of sensible agreement on how to treat the matter. That is why we are prepared to contribute our consent to the passage of this Bill in the Parliament of Canada, so that the measures can be implemented.
In the course of deciding what action to take, we have to point out those things of real importance to the taxpayers who will be affected by this convention. First, there is the matter of
June 22, 1984

freedom of information. Every taxpayer in Canada, including the House Leader for the Liberal Party if he gets involved in any cross border events, will be subjected to the application of this convention and the provisions of the convention. As a Canadian dealing with matters in the United States, information concerning his fears will be a public record. Under the provisions of the convention, the United States authorities will have full access to that information. They can require any information that they normally require in the enforcement of their tax measures. That will be on file in the United States of America. That may not bother the House Leader for the Liberal Party, but there are some Canadians who do not particularly want all their files in Washington, the capital of the United States, or any other place.
We have seen the other side of that. Canadian Pacific, that great Canadian company, files documents and other materials with the Government of Canada under legislation of the Parliament of Canada under which the corporation is constituted. However, they do not tell us anything about their inside activities, trading in shares and that sort of thing which they are required to disclose in the United States. If you want to find out anything about Canadian Pacific, the salaries of its directors and officers and other inside information, do not come to Ottawa, the capital of Canada. Go to Washington. You will get it there. They have all kinds of information.
There is an exchange of information. The provisions of the convention provide for free flow of information. I could look up the specific provision. It is Article XXVII headed "Exchange of Information". I could read it, but why should I? Let the member from the New Democratic Party read it on his own. I will just note for the record of the House of Commons that there is a provision in the convention relating to the exchange of information.
This means that information concerning Canadian taxpayers who find themselves subject to this convention can flow freely to the United States of America to be held in their information banks. Under their freedom of information laws, which we do not have in Canada, anybody in Canada can probably gain access to much of that information. That is an important point to consider. It is not all one way. We are giving up some things here. That may be acceptable in the broad concern of avoiding double taxation.
There are very specific things that we do not have time to look into. As I indicated, it may not even be the function of Members of the House of Commons to look into them. It has been pointed out to me that these provisions may pass to United States companies and small business enterprises the benefits intended to be granted to Canadian small business and enterprises with respect to the special tax concessions recently granted. As I understand it, corporations and persons subject to these convention measures are entitled to the lowest form of taxation. Consequently, if a United States business concern becomes subject to the provisions of this convention, I understand it will be entitled to the benefits that would flow through to a small business enterprise in Canada.
Tax Convention Act
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) recently introduced a budget in the House of Commons that had special specific measures designed to encourage Canadian small business. As a result of this convention, those same benefits would flow through to a U.S. enterprise to which the convention was subject. In other words, we have agreed in this Bill and convention to pass on to the United States concerns and enterprises to which the convention applies the same benefits that we give to Canadians. Of course, in exchange we will be getting in the United States, as I understand it, similar benefits. We must be aware of that reciprocity.
The Government of Canada as one of its stated policies has tried to encourage Canadian ownership, Canadian control of our own economy. Here is a measure that is going the other way. We are saying "Look, let's share this continent, this part of North America in economic terms." I would say that is a contradiction in Government policy, but not one with which I have any special agreement. I believe there has to be free commerce, free exchange, with protective provisions, of course. We should be moving in that direction. That is the effect of the convention. The effect of approving Bill S-14 will be to give consent and concurrence to a legislative directive.
I think I have indicated what I have set out to do; first and foremost that we want to participate and co-operate in the process by which conventions negotiated between officers of the Government of Canada and officers of the Government of the United States are ratified and implemented. We do not want to block the measures. We do not take it as our parliamentary duty to examine the provisions with a fine toothcomb. We do not take it as our function to undo what has already been done and agreed to, but we do take it as our responsibility to review in a general way the situation to make sure there is nothing blatant, improper or unfair in the provisions, to the extent that we have that capacity, and then give it approval in that spirit of co-operation.
It is quite different from our attitude toward Bill C-9 where we thought that the liberty of the subject in Canada was at stake and that there were other vital matters relating to personal freedoms at stake. This is simply an administrative measure. We recognize that. We want to co-operate, but we want to give a warning that we should watch this sort of thing carefully. We should watch the provisions. There may be effects of which we are not aware. We could have repeats of situations like Georges Bank.
Why do we give things away when we should be bargaining? How did this process with respect to the convention on Georges Bank come about? Did anyone speak to the Senator from Rhode Island beforehand to find out what he thought? Did anyone go to Kennedy to find out that this opposition existed before we gave our interests away? That situation will probably not arise at all with respect to this tax convention, but, as the Parliamentary Secretary said, no approval has been given through Congress. How do we know that that approval will be given? How do we know they will not hold up that

June 22, 1984
Tax Convention Act
approval for some other concession that is part of the international bargaining arrangements and so on?
In a sense, we approve this Bill with a blind eye. I make no apology for that because that is the way our system works. As I said, it is the spirit of co-operation that is important. It is important to get the business that is in the interests of the public and the Canadian taxpayers done. That is why we reviewed the Bill and that is why we are prepared to give it consent. Once again, we are placing faith in the Government of Canada. People may say that it is a mistake to do so, that we should not even think of doing so. However, under our system we must place faith in the Government of Canada.
I for one, on behalf of the Progressive Conservative Party, can only say that we are going to do it once, we are going to place faith in the Government of Canada. We have been told that this measure benefits the people of Canada in relation to taxation and we accept the word of the Government. We consent to the processing of this Bill as quickly as possible so that it can be approved by the appropriate authorities and given effect, in the hope and expectation that it will benefit taxpayers in Canada.

speechtext: Bill C-36, to amend the Interest Act, is before the House. That Bill would give people a break on the interest rates of their mortgages. I thought we would deal with that this afternoon. Through you, Mr. Speaker, perhaps the government House Leader could tell us what is about to happen with that Bill. Could it be dealt with this afternoon, or will it be dealt with expeditiously next week? I have not been informed about that, and I see no reason to give unanimous consent until I am informed.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1984 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we had scheduled Bill C-37 to be debated today, and I wanted to see that Bill passed. However, we succeeded in passing three Bills today which are most important-the GIS Bill, the Mortgage Protection Plan and Bill S-14, the Tax Convention Act between Canada and the United States.
I thank the Hon. Member for his comments and his generous offer to allow the Bill to amend the Interest Act to be adopted. Unfortunately it is past four o'clock and it is time for Private Members' Business. That would require the unanimous consent of the House. If we had unanimous consent to pass the Bill which amends the Interest Act before five o'clock we would agree to that. However, it has not been discussed among the House Leaders that the House should sit beyond four o'clock to deal with Government business. There were meetings yesterday and the day before with the House Leaders. The House Leader for the Progressive Conservative Party is here, however the House Leader for the NDP had to leave, and I understand he had a very good reason for doing so. I would not like to force something on the Official Opposition without having consulted with them. However, if they are willing to sit spontaneously and deal with the Interest Act, fine. If not, I am not in a position to blame anyone because the time provided to deal with Government business has expired.

Business of the House
I thank the Hon. Member for his generosity. If we do not receive consent today, then maybe next week we will be successful in including this piece of legislation because of the trend which seems to be developing now. That trend will show the people of the country that Parliament can work and that it will adjourn on June 29 with a number of very important Bills passed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1984 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it never ceases to amaze me that the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) sits in oblivion of what is happening in this House. This is another demonstration of the Member again speaking without having the slightest idea of what he is talking about. Of course, he proposes to speak on behalf of the NDP. That is easy for him to say. Where is his House Leader? Can he assure me that he has spoken with his House Leader about the order of business for today, and the matters which have been discussed in confidence with the Government House Leader regarding the way in which this legislation will be proceeded with? I suggest not, Sir.
We have tried to pass a lot of legislation. We have been successful in passing several pieces of legislation here today. For the Member for Vancouver-Kingsway to attempt to grandstand himself before the 20 or 30 people in the galleries here today is typical of the level of his participation in this House. I would say to him that if he wants to find out what is going on he should consult with the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans).
We have discussed the order of business and the sequence on the floor of the House of Commons. I know who is standing in his place and wants to speak on the interest Bill. He only began his remarks. It was not a Member of my Party, it was the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper) who had the floor of the House. I suppose, miraculously, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway will stand in his place and tell us that he has had a transcendental discussion with the Member from Winnipeg-St. James and finds that he does not want to say anything further. The last time this Bill was up, he just cleared his throat. He had the floor when the House adjourned. When the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway stands up and tries to suggest that we are holding up legislation which is helpful to the people of Canada, I would remind him that these allegations are contrary to the truth-to put it in parliamentary terms. I think that he should allow the House
Leaders to carry on with these negotiations and that he should not grandstand during the last days of a dying session. We are all nervous about the election. We are all trembling in our places and wondering about our own seats-particularly the Member for Vancouver-Kingsway.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1984 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: We are not.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1984 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Of course the Government House Leader would not be worried. He comes from what is known as a rotten borough. That is what he told me. He told me, "No problem. I don't care. People will re-elect me because I am so wonderful". I take my re-election seriously. I would simply say to the Member that I do not appreciate being accused of doing things which are detrimental to the people of Canada. If it comes down to it, I will put my record against his any time.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1984 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not need to be lectured by the Opposition House Leader as to my record or position. I would be prepared to listen to the Government House Leader, who properly put the matter into perspective. He suggested that they were prepared to go ahead. I was prepared to agree with him, but after hearing the arguments and the insults of the Opposition House Leader, and after seeing that this Bill in fact changes interest rates and helps the real people of the world who badly need this legislation because they are paying 17 per cent and 18 per cent interest rates on their mortgages- and they are locked into those mortgages-I am seeking the unanimous consent of the House, and I have spoken with my House Leader and the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper), to proceed with this Bill now.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1984 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Order, please. Is there unanimous consent for the proposal of the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TAX CONVENTION ACT, 1984 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: No, there is not. I am sad to say that the Hon. Member did not consult with the House Leader for the New Democratic Party, contrary to what he has said. Under the circumstances, I refuse to give unanimous consent.
